/></a></span></div><div class="thumbcaption"><i><a href="/wiki/The_Bad_Man_(1941_film)" title="The Bad Man (1941 film)">The Bad Man</a></i> (1941)</div></div></div></div></div>
<p>After obtaining a <a href="/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts" title="Bachelor of Arts">Bachelor of Arts</a> degree in <a href="/wiki/Economics" title="Economics">economics</a> and <a href="/wiki/Sociology" title="Sociology">sociology</a> from Eureka College in 1932,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMullen1999207_27-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMullen1999207-27">&#91;27&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-28" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-28">&#91;28&#93;</a></sup> Reagan took a job in <a href="/wiki/Davenport,_Iowa" title="Davenport, Iowa">Davenport, Iowa</a>, as a sports broadcaster for four football games in the <a href="/wiki/Big_Ten_Conference" title="Big Ten Conference">Big Ten Conference</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands201524–26_29-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands201524–26-29">&#91;29&#93;</a></sup> He then worked for <a href="/wiki/WHO_(AM)" title="WHO (AM)">WHO radio</a> in <a href="/wiki/Des_Moines" class="mw-redirect" title="Des Moines">Des Moines</a> as a broadcaster for the <a href="/wiki/Chicago_Cubs" title="Chicago Cubs">Chicago Cubs</a>. His specialty was creating play-by-play accounts of games using only basic descriptions that the station received by wire as the games were in progress.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands201529–30_30-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands201529–30-30">&#91;30&#93;</a></sup> Simultaneously, he often expressed his opposition to racism.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2000458_31-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2000458-31">&#91;31&#93;</a></sup> In 1936, while traveling with the Cubs to their spring training in California, Reagan took a screen test that led to a seven-year contract with <a href="/wiki/Warner_Bros." title="Warner Bros.">Warner Bros.</a><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard201218–19_32-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard201218–19-32">&#91;32&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Reagan arrived at <a href="/wiki/Hollywood,_Los_Angeles" title="Hollywood, Los Angeles">Hollywood</a> in 1937, debuting in <i><a href="/wiki/Love_Is_on_the_Air" title="Love Is on the Air">Love Is on the Air</a></i> (1937).<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands201539–40_33-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands201539–40-33">&#91;33&#93;</a></sup> Using a simple and direct approach to acting and following his directors' instructions,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFreie201543–44_34-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreie201543–44-34">&#91;34&#93;</a></sup> Reagan made thirty films, mostly <a href="/wiki/B_films" class="mw-redirect" title="B films">B films</a>, before beginning <a href="/wiki/Military_service" title="Military service">military service</a> in April 1942.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEVaughn199430_35-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVaughn199430-35">&#91;35&#93;</a></sup> He broke out of these types of films by portraying <a href="/wiki/George_Gipp" title="George Gipp">George Gipp</a> in <i><a href="/wiki/Knute_Rockne,_All_American" title="Knute Rockne, All American">Knute Rockne, All American</a></i> (1940), which would be rejuvenated when reporters called Reagan "the Gipper" while he campaigned for president of the United States.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon200113–15_36-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon200113–15-36">&#91;36&#93;</a></sup> Afterward, Reagan starred in <i><a href="/wiki/Kings_Row" title="Kings Row">Kings Row</a></i> (1942) as a leg amputee, asking, "Where's the rest of me?"<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard201225–26_37-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard201225–26-37">&#91;37&#93;</a></sup> His performance was considered his best by many critics.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEVaughn199437_38-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVaughn199437-38">&#91;38&#93;</a></sup> Reagan became a star,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFriedrich199789_39-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFriedrich199789-39">&#91;39&#93;</a></sup> with <a href="/wiki/Gallup_polls" class="mw-redirect" title="Gallup polls">Gallup polls</a> placing him "in the top 100 stars" from 1941 to 1942.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEVaughn199437_38-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVaughn199437-38">&#91;38&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/World_War_II" title="World War II">World War II</a> interrupted the movie stardom that Reagan would never be able to achieve again<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFriedrich199789_39-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFriedrich199789-39">&#91;39&#93;</a></sup> as <a href="/wiki/Warner_Bros." title="Warner Bros.">Warner Bros.</a> became uncertain about his ability to generate ticket sales. Reagan, who had a limited acting range, was dissatisfied with the roles he received. As a result, <a href="/wiki/Lew_Wasserman" title="Lew Wasserman">Lew Wasserman</a> renegotiated his contract with his studio, allowing him to also make films with <a href="/wiki/Universal_Pictures" title="Universal Pictures">Universal Pictures</a>, <a href="/wiki/Paramount_Pictures" title="Paramount Pictures">Paramount Pictures</a>, and <a href="/wiki/RKO_Pictures" title="RKO Pictures">RKO Pictures</a> as a freelancer. With this, Reagan appeared in multiple <a href="/wiki/Western_film" title="Western film">western films</a>, something that had been denied him working at Warner Bros.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon200359_40-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon200359-40">&#91;40&#93;</a></sup> In 1952, he ended his relationship with Warner Bros.,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEVaughn1994236_41-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVaughn1994236-41">&#91;41&#93;</a></sup> but went on to appear in a total of 53 films,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEVaughn199430_35-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVaughn199430-35">&#91;35&#93;</a></sup> his last being <i><a href="/wiki/The_Killers_(1964_film)" title="The Killers (1964 film)">The Killers</a></i> (1964).<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEVaughn1994312_42-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVaughn1994312-42">&#91;42&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Military_service">Military service</span></h3>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Reagan_FMPU.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Captain Reagan in the Army Air Force working for the 1st Motion Picture Unit in Culver City, California, between 1943 and 1944" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ef/Reagan_FMPU.jpg/220px-Reagan_FMPU.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="172" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ef/Reagan_FMPU.jpg/330px-Reagan_FMPU.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ef/Reagan_FMPU.jpg/440px-Reagan_FMPU.jpg 2x" data-file-width="520" data-file-height="406" /></a><figcaption>Reagan at <a href="/wiki/First_Motion_Picture_Unit#Life_at_Fort_Roach" title="First Motion Picture Unit">Fort Roach</a>, between 1943 and 1944</figcaption></figure>
<p>In April 1937, Reagan enlisted in the <a href="/wiki/United_States_Army_Reserve" title="United States Army Reserve">United States Army Reserve</a>. He was assigned as <a href="/wiki/Private_(rank)" title="Private (rank)">a private</a> in Des Moines' <a href="/wiki/322nd_Cavalry_Regiment_(United_States)" title="322nd Cavalry Regiment (United States)">322nd Cavalry Regiment</a> and reassigned to <a href="/wiki/Second_lieutenant" title="Second lieutenant">second lieutenant</a> in the Officers Reserve Corps.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEOliverMarion2010148_43-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOliverMarion2010148-43">&#91;43&#93;</a></sup> He later became a part of the <a href="/wiki/323rd_Cavalry_Regiment_(United_States)" title="323rd Cavalry Regiment (United States)">323rd Cavalry Regiment</a> in California.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEVaughn199496_44-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVaughn199496-44">&#91;44&#93;</a></sup> As relations between the United States and <a href="/wiki/Japan" title="Japan">Japan</a> worsened, Reagan was ordered for active duty while he was filming <a href="/wiki/Kings_Row" title="Kings Row"><i>Kings Row</i>.</a> Wasserman and Warner Bros. <a href="/wiki/Lawyer" title="Lawyer">lawyers</a> successfully sent draft deferments to complete the film in October 1941. However, to avoid accusations of Reagan being a <a href="/wiki/Draft_evasion" title="Draft evasion">draft dodger</a>, the studio let him go in April 1942.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard201226Brands201554–55_45-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard201226Brands201554–55-45">&#91;45&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Reagan reported for duty with severe <a href="/wiki/Near-sightedness" title="Near-sightedness">near-sightedness.</a> His first assignment was at <a href="/wiki/Fort_Mason" title="Fort Mason">Fort Mason</a> as a <a href="/wiki/Liaison_officer" title="Liaison officer">liaison officer</a>, a role that allowed him to transfer to the <a href="/wiki/United_States_Army_Air_Forces" title="United States Army Air Forces">United States Army Air Forces</a> (AAF). Reagan became an AAF <a href="/wiki/Public_relations" title="Public relations">public relations</a> officer and was subsequently assigned to the <a href="/wiki/18th_AAF_Base_Unit" class="mw-redirect" title="18th AAF Base Unit">18th AAF Base Unit</a> in <a href="/wiki/Culver_City" class="mw-redirect" title="Culver City">Culver City</a><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEOliverMarion2010148–149_46-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOliverMarion2010148–149-46">&#91;46&#93;</a></sup> where he felt that it was "impossible to remove an incompetent or lazy worker" due to what he felt was "the incompetence, the delays, and inefficiencies" of the federal <a href="/wiki/Bureaucracy" title="Bureaucracy">bureaucracy.</a><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard201227_47-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard201227-47">&#91;47&#93;</a></sup> Despite this, Reagan participated in the Provisional Task Force Show Unit <a href="/wiki/Burbank,_California" title="Burbank, California">in Burbank</a><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEOliverMarion2010149_48-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOliverMarion2010149-48">&#91;48&#93;</a></sup> and continued to make theatrical films.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands201557_49-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands201557-49">&#91;49&#93;</a></sup> He was also ordered to temporary duty in <a href="/wiki/New_York_City" title="New York City">New York City</a> to participate in the <a href="/wiki/Series_E_bond" title="Series E bond">sixth War Loan Drive</a> before being reassigned to <a href="/wiki/Fort_MacArthur" title="Fort MacArthur">Fort MacArthur</a> until his discharge on December 9, 1945, as <a href="/wiki/Captain_(United_States_O-3)" title="Captain (United States O-3)">a captain</a>. Throughout his military service, Reagan produced over 400 training films.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEOliverMarion2010149_48-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOliverMarion2010149-48">&#91;48&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Screen_Actors_Guild_presidency">Screen Actors Guild presidency</span></h3>
<p>When <a href="/wiki/Robert_Montgomery_(actor)" title="Robert Montgomery (actor)">Robert Montgomery</a> resigned as president of the <a href="/wiki/Screen_Actors_Guild" title="Screen Actors Guild">Screen Actors Guild</a> (SAG) on March 10, 1947, Reagan was elected to that position, in a special election.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon200386_50-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon200386-50">&#91;50&#93;</a></sup> Reagan's first tenure saw various labor-management disputes,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEVaughn1994133_51-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVaughn1994133-51">&#91;51&#93;</a></sup> the <a href="/wiki/Hollywood_blacklist" title="Hollywood blacklist">Hollywood blacklist</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEVaughn1994146_52-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVaughn1994146-52">&#91;52&#93;</a></sup> and the <a href="/wiki/Taft%E2%80%93Hartley_Act" title="Taft–Hartley Act">Taft–Hartley Act</a>'s implementation.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEVaughn1994154_53-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVaughn1994154-53">&#91;53&#93;</a></sup> On April 10, the <a href="/wiki/Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation" title="Federal Bureau of Investigation">Federal Bureau of Investigation</a> (FBI) interviewed Reagan and he provided them with the names of actors whom he believed to be <a href="/wiki/Communist_sympathizers" class="mw-redirect" title="Communist sympathizers">communist sympathizers</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton199832_54-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton199832-54">&#91;54&#93;</a></sup> During a <a href="/wiki/House_Un-American_Activities_Committee" title="House Un-American Activities Committee">House Un-American Activities Committee</a> hearing, Reagan testified that some guild members were associated with the <a href="/wiki/Communist_Party_USA" title="Communist Party USA">Communist Party</a><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon200397_55-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon200397-55">&#91;55&#93;</a></sup> and that he was well-informed on a "jurisdictional strike".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon200398_56-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon200398-56">&#91;56&#93;</a></sup> When asked if he was aware of communist efforts within the <a href="/wiki/Screen_Writers_Guild" title="Screen Writers Guild">Screen Writers Guild</a>, he called the efforts "hearsay".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands201589_57-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands201589-57">&#91;57&#93;</a></sup> Reagan would remain SAG president until he resigned on November 10, 1952;<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEEliot2008266_58-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEliot2008266-58">&#91;58&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Walter_Pidgeon" title="Walter Pidgeon">Walter Pidgeon</a> succeeded him, but Reagan stayed on the board.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEVaughn1994179_59-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVaughn1994179-59">&#91;59&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The SAG fought with <a href="/wiki/Film_producer" title="Film producer">film producers</a> over <a href="/wiki/Residual_(entertainment_industry)" title="Residual (entertainment industry)">residual payments</a><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton199835_60-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton199835-60">&#91;60&#93;</a></sup> and on November 16, 1959, the board installed Reagan as SAG president,<sup id="cite_ref-61" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-61">&#91;61&#93;</a></sup> replacing the resigned <a href="/wiki/Howard_Keel" title="Howard Keel">Howard Keel</a>. In his second stint, Reagan managed to secure the payments for actors whose theatrical films were released from 1948 to 1959 and subsequently televised. The producers were initially required to pay the actors fees, but they ultimately settled for pensions instead. However, they were still required to pay residuals for films after 1959. Reagan resigned from the SAG presidency on June 7, 1960, and also left the board;<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2003111–112_62-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2003111–112-62">&#91;62&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/George_Chandler" title="George Chandler">George Chandler</a> succeeded him as SAG president.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTELandesman2015173_63-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTELandesman2015173-63">&#91;63&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Marriages_and_children">Marriages and children</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1096954695/mw-parser-output/.tmulti"><div class="thumb tmulti tright"><div class="thumbinner multiimageinner" style="width:392px;max-width:392px"><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:177px;max-width:177px"><div class="thumbimage" style="height:167px;overflow:hidden"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Wyman_%26_Reagan.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Actors Jane Wyman and Ronald Reagan at a Los Angeles premiere for the 1942 film Tales of Manhattan" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/Wyman_%26_Reagan.jpg/175px-Wyman_%26_Reagan.jpg" decoding="async" width="175" height="168" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/Wyman_%26_Reagan.jpg/263px-Wyman_%26_Reagan.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/Wyman_%26_Reagan.jpg/350px-Wyman_%26_Reagan.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3841" data-file-height="3683" /></a></span></div><div class="thumbcaption">Reagan and Jane Wyman, 1942</div></div><div class="tsingle" style="width:211px;max-width:211px"><div class="thumbimage" style="height:167px;overflow:hidden"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:The_Reagan%27s_at_the_Stork_Club_in_New_York_City.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="The Reagans at The Stork Club in New York City, 1952" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f3/The_Reagan%27s_at_the_Stork_Club_in_New_York_City.jpg/209px-The_Reagan%27s_at_the_Stork_Club_in_New_York_City.jpg" decoding="async" width="209" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f3/The_Reagan%27s_at_the_Stork_Club_in_New_York_City.jpg/314px-The_Reagan%27s_at_the_Stork_Club_in_New_York_City.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f3/The_Reagan%27s_at_the_Stork_Club_in_New_York_City.jpg/418px-The_Reagan%27s_at_the_Stork_Club_in_New_York_City.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4000" data-file-height="3202" /></a></span></div><div class="thumbcaption">Ronald and Nancy Reagan, 1952</div></div></div></div></div>
<p>Reagan married <i><a href="/wiki/Brother_Rat" title="Brother Rat">Brother Rat</a></i> (1938) co-star <a href="/wiki/Jane_Wyman" title="Jane Wyman">Jane Wyman</a><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands201543_64-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands201543-64">&#91;64&#93;</a></sup> in January 1940.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard201223_65-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard201223-65">&#91;65&#93;</a></sup> Together, they had two biological daughters: <a href="/wiki/Maureen_Reagan" title="Maureen Reagan">Maureen</a> in 1941,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard201225_66-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard201225-66">&#91;66&#93;</a></sup> and Christine,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDick201488_67-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDick201488-67">&#91;67&#93;</a></sup> born prematurely and dead the next day in 1947.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard201229_68-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard201229-68">&#91;68&#93;</a></sup> They adopted one son, <a href="/wiki/Michael_Reagan" title="Michael Reagan">Michael</a>, in 1945.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard201227_47-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard201227-47">&#91;47&#93;</a></sup> Wyman filed to <a href="/wiki/Divorce" title="Divorce">divorce</a> Reagan in June 1948. She was uninterested in politics, and occasionally recriminated, reconciled and <a href="/wiki/Marital_separation" title="Marital separation">separated</a> with him. Although Reagan was unprepared,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard201229_68-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard201229-68">&#91;68&#93;</a></sup> the divorce was finalized in July 1949. Reagan would also remain close to his children.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon200373–74_69-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon200373–74-69">&#91;69&#93;</a></sup> Later that year, Reagan met <a href="/wiki/Nancy_Davis" class="mw-redirect" title="Nancy Davis">Nancy Davis</a> after she contacted him in his capacity as the SAG president about her name appearing on a communist <a href="/wiki/Blacklisting" title="Blacklisting">blacklist</a> in Hollywood; she had been mistaken for another Nancy Davis.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015109_70-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015109-70">&#91;70&#93;</a></sup> They married in March 1952<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015113_71-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015113-71">&#91;71&#93;</a></sup> and had two children, <a href="/wiki/Patti_Davis" title="Patti Davis">Patti</a> in 1952, and <a href="/wiki/Ron_Reagan" title="Ron Reagan">Ron</a> in 1958.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015199_72-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015199-72">&#91;72&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Television">Television</span></h3>
<p>Reagan became the <a href="/wiki/Television_presenter" title="Television presenter">host</a> of <a href="/wiki/MCA_Inc." title="MCA Inc.">MCA Inc.</a> television production <i><a href="/wiki/General_Electric_Theater" title="General Electric Theater">General Electric Theater</a></i><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEVaughn1994236_41-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVaughn1994236-41">&#91;41&#93;</a></sup> at Wasserman's recommendation. It featured multiple guest stars,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015120_73-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015120-73">&#91;73&#93;</a></sup> and Ronald and Nancy Reagan, continuing to use her stage name Nancy Davis, acted together in three episodes.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMetzger198926_74-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMetzger198926-74">&#91;74&#93;</a></sup> When asked how Reagan was able to recruit such stars to appear on the show during television's infancy, he replied, "Good stories, top direction, production quality."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015122_75-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015122-75">&#91;75&#93;</a></sup> However, the viewership declined in the 1960s and the show was canceled in 1962.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015131–132_76-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015131–132-76">&#91;76&#93;</a></sup> In 1965, Reagan became the host<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015145_77-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015145-77">&#91;77&#93;</a></sup> of another MCA production, <i><a href="/wiki/Death_Valley_Days" title="Death Valley Days">Death Valley Days</a></i>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton199836_78-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton199836-78">&#91;78&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Early_political_activities">Early political activities</span></h2>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Goldwater-Reagan_in_1964.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Reagan speaking for presidential candidate Barry Goldwater in Los Angeles, 1964" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/30/Goldwater-Reagan_in_1964.jpg/220px-Goldwater-Reagan_in_1964.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="153" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/30/Goldwater-Reagan_in_1964.jpg/330px-Goldwater-Reagan_in_1964.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/30/Goldwater-Reagan_in_1964.jpg/440px-Goldwater-Reagan_in_1964.jpg 2x" data-file-width="689" data-file-height="478" /></a><figcaption>Reagan campaigning with <a href="/wiki/Barry_Goldwater_1964_presidential_campaign" title="Barry Goldwater 1964 presidential campaign">Barry Goldwater</a>, 1964</figcaption></figure>
<p>Reagan began as a <a href="/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States)" title="Democratic Party (United States)">Democrat</a>, viewing <a href="/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt" title="Franklin D. Roosevelt">Franklin D. Roosevelt</a> as "a true hero".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEYager200612–13_79-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYager200612–13-79">&#91;79&#93;</a></sup> He joined <a href="/wiki/American_Veterans_Committee_(1943%E2%80%932008)" title="American Veterans Committee (1943–2008)">the American Veterans Committee</a> and <a href="/wiki/Hollywood_Independent_Citizens_Committee_of_the_Arts,_Sciences_and_Professions" class="mw-redirect" title="Hollywood Independent Citizens Committee of the Arts, Sciences and Professions">Hollywood Independent Citizens Committee of the Arts, Sciences and Professions</a> (HICCASP), worked with the <a href="/wiki/AFL%E2%80%93CIO" class="mw-redirect" title="AFL–CIO">AFL–CIO</a> to fight <a href="/wiki/Right-to-work_law" title="Right-to-work law">right-to-work laws</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard201228_80-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard201228-80">&#91;80&#93;</a></sup> and continued to speak out against racism when he was in Hollywood.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998139_81-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998139-81">&#91;81&#93;</a></sup> In 1945, Reagan planned to lead an HICCASP anti-nuclear rally, but Warner Bros. prevented him from going.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTELettow20064–5_82-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTELettow20064–5-82">&#91;82&#93;</a></sup> In 1946, he appeared in a radio program called <i>Operation Terror</i> to speak out against rising <a href="/wiki/Ku_Klux_Klan" title="Ku Klux Klan">Ku Klux Klan</a> activity in the country, citing the attacks as a "capably organized systematic campaign of fascist violence and intimidation and horror".<sup id="cite_ref-Racism_83-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Racism-83">&#91;83&#93;</a></sup> Reagan also supported <a href="/wiki/Harry_S._Truman" title="Harry S. Truman">Harry S. Truman</a> in <a href="/wiki/1948_United_States_presidential_election" title="1948 United States presidential election">the 1948 presidential election</a><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard201249_84-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard201249-84">&#91;84&#93;</a></sup> and <a href="/wiki/Helen_Gahagan_Douglas" title="Helen Gahagan Douglas">Helen Gahagan Douglas</a> for the United States Senate <a href="/wiki/1950_United_States_Senate_election_in_California" title="1950 United States Senate election in California">in 1950</a>. It was Reagan's belief that communism was a powerful backstage influence in Hollywood that led him to rally his friends against them.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard201228_80-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard201228-80">&#91;80&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Reagan began shifting to the right when he supported the presidential campaigns of <a href="/wiki/Dwight_D._Eisenhower" title="Dwight D. Eisenhower">Dwight D. Eisenhower</a> in 1952 and <a href="/wiki/Richard_Nixon" title="Richard Nixon">Richard Nixon</a> in 1960.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon200053_85-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon200053-85">&#91;85&#93;</a></sup> When Reagan was contracted by <a href="/wiki/General_Electric" title="General Electric">General Electric</a> (GE), he gave speeches to their employees. His speeches had a positive take on <a href="/wiki/Free_market" title="Free market">free markets</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard201242–43_86-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard201242–43-86">&#91;86&#93;</a></sup> Under GE vice president <a href="/wiki/Lemuel_Boulware" title="Lemuel Boulware">Lemuel Boulware</a>, a staunch anti-communist,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEEvans200621_87-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans200621-87">&#91;87&#93;</a></sup> employees were encouraged to vote for business-friendly politicians.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEEvans20064_88-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans20064-88">&#91;88&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 1961, Reagan adapted his speeches into <a href="/wiki/Ronald_Reagan_Speaks_Out_Against_Socialized_Medicine" title="Ronald Reagan Speaks Out Against Socialized Medicine">another speech</a> to criticize <a href="/wiki/Medicare_(United_States)" title="Medicare (United States)">Medicare</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESkidmore2008103_89-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESkidmore2008103-89">&#91;89&#93;</a></sup> In his view, its legislation would have meant "the end of <a href="/wiki/Individual_freedom" class="mw-redirect" title="Individual freedom">individual freedom</a> in the United States".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEOnge2017240_90-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOnge2017240-90">&#91;90&#93;</a></sup> In 1962, Reagan was dropped by GE,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2003112_91-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2003112-91">&#91;91&#93;</a></sup> and he formally registered as <a href="/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States)" title="Republican Party (United States)">a Republican</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon200053_85-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon200053-85">&#91;85&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 1964, Reagan gave a speech for presidential contender <a href="/wiki/Barry_Goldwater" title="Barry Goldwater">Barry Goldwater</a><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard201255_92-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard201255-92">&#91;92&#93;</a></sup> that was eventually referred to as "<a href="/wiki/A_Time_for_Choosing" title="A Time for Choosing">A Time for Choosing</a>".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2003132_93-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2003132-93">&#91;93&#93;</a></sup>  Reagan argued that <a href="/wiki/Founding_Fathers_of_the_United_States" title="Founding Fathers of the United States">the Founding Fathers</a> "knew that governments don't control things. And they knew when a government sets out to do that, it must use force and coercion to achieve its purpose"<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReagan199027_94-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReagan199027-94">&#91;94&#93;</a></sup> and that "We've been told increasingly that we must choose between left or right."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReagan199099–100_95-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReagan199099–100-95">&#91;95&#93;</a></sup> Even though the speech was not enough to turn around the faltering <a href="/wiki/Barry_Goldwater_1964_presidential_campaign" title="Barry Goldwater 1964 presidential campaign">Goldwater campaign</a>, it increased Reagan's profile among conservatives. <a href="/wiki/David_S._Broder" title="David S. Broder">David S. Broder</a> and <a href="/wiki/Stephen_H._Hess" title="Stephen H. Hess">Stephen H. Hess</a> called it "the most successful national political debut since <a href="/wiki/William_Jennings_Bryan" title="William Jennings Bryan">William Jennings Bryan</a> electrified the <a href="/wiki/1896_Democratic_National_Convention" title="1896 Democratic National Convention">1896 Democratic convention</a> with his famous <a href="/wiki/Cross_of_Gold_speech" title="Cross of Gold speech">'Cross of Gold' address</a>".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard201255_92-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard201255-92">&#91;92&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="1966_California_gubernatorial_election">1966 California gubernatorial election</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/1966_California_gubernatorial_election" title="1966 California gubernatorial election">1966 California gubernatorial election</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Ronald_Reagan_and_Nancy_Reagan_at_victory_celebration_for_1966_Governor%27s_election_(cropped).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="The Reagans celebrating Ronald&#39;s victory in the 1966 California gubernatorial election at The Biltmore Hotel in Los Angeles" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/Ronald_Reagan_and_Nancy_Reagan_at_victory_celebration_for_1966_Governor%27s_election_%28cropped%29.jpg/220px-Ronald_Reagan_and_Nancy_Reagan_at_victory_celebration_for_1966_Governor%27s_election_%28cropped%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="145" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/Ronald_Reagan_and_Nancy_Reagan_at_victory_celebration_for_1966_Governor%27s_election_%28cropped%29.jpg/330px-Ronald_Reagan_and_Nancy_Reagan_at_victory_celebration_for_1966_Governor%27s_election_%28cropped%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/Ronald_Reagan_and_Nancy_Reagan_at_victory_celebration_for_1966_Governor%27s_election_%28cropped%29.jpg/440px-Ronald_Reagan_and_Nancy_Reagan_at_victory_celebration_for_1966_Governor%27s_election_%28cropped%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3185" data-file-height="2098" /></a><figcaption>Ronald and Nancy Reagan celebrating his gubernatorial election victory, 1966</figcaption></figure>
<p>In January 1966, Reagan announced his candidacy for the California governorship,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2003141_96-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2003141-96">&#91;96&#93;</a></sup> repeating his stances on individual freedom and <a href="/wiki/Big_government" title="Big government">big government</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015148_97-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015148-97">&#91;97&#93;</a></sup> When he met with black Republicans in March,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015149_98-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015149-98">&#91;98&#93;</a></sup> he was criticized for opposing the <a href="/wiki/Civil_Rights_Act_of_1964" title="Civil Rights Act of 1964">Civil Rights Act of 1964</a>. Certain in his own lack of prejudice, Reagan responded resentfully that bigotry was not in his nature<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2003142_99-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2003142-99">&#91;99&#93;</a></sup> and later argued that certain provisions of the act infringed upon the rights of property owners.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015150_100-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015150-100">&#91;100&#93;</a></sup> After the <a href="/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_California" title="Supreme Court of California">Supreme Court of California</a> ruled that the initiative that repealed the <a href="/wiki/Rumford_Act" class="mw-redirect" title="Rumford Act">Rumford Act</a> was unconstitutional in May, he voiced his support for the act's repeal,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2003147_101-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2003147-101">&#91;101&#93;</a></sup> but later preferred amending it.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPutnam200627_102-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPutnam200627-102">&#91;102&#93;</a></sup> In the Republican primary, Reagan defeated <a href="/wiki/George_Christopher_(mayor)" title="George Christopher (mayor)">George Christopher</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2003147–148_103-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2003147–148-103">&#91;103&#93;</a></sup> a moderate<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2003135_104-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2003135-104">&#91;104&#93;</a></sup> who <a href="/wiki/William_F._Buckley_Jr." title="William F. Buckley Jr.">William F. Buckley Jr.</a> thought had painted Reagan as extreme.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015148_97-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015148-97">&#91;97&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Reagan's general election opponent, incumbent governor <a href="/wiki/Pat_Brown" title="Pat Brown">Pat Brown</a>, attempted to label Reagan as an extremist and tout his own accomplishments.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton199869_105-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton199869-105">&#91;105&#93;</a></sup> Reagan portrayed himself as a political outsider,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2003149_106-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2003149-106">&#91;106&#93;</a></sup> and charged Brown as responsible for the <a href="/wiki/Watts_riots" title="Watts riots">Watts riots</a> and lenient on crime.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton199869_105-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton199869-105">&#91;105&#93;</a></sup> In numerous speeches, Reagan "hit the Brown administration about high taxes, uncontrolled spending, the radicals at the <a href="/wiki/University_of_California,_Berkeley" title="University of California, Berkeley">University of California, Berkeley</a>, and the need for <a href="/wiki/Accountability" title="Accountability">accountability</a> in government".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard201259_107-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard201259-107">&#91;107&#93;</a></sup> Meanwhile, many in the press perceived Reagan as "monumentally ignorant of state issues", though <a href="/wiki/Lou_Cannon" title="Lou Cannon">Lou Cannon</a> said that Reagan benefited from an appearance he and Brown made on <i><a href="/wiki/Meet_the_Press" title="Meet the Press">Meet the Press</a></i> in September.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2003158–159_108-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2003158–159-108">&#91;108&#93;</a></sup> Ultimately, Reagan won the governorship with 57 percent of the vote compared to Brown's 42 percent.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard201260_109-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard201260-109">&#91;109&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span id="1967.E2.80.931975:_California_governorship"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="1967–1975:_California_governorship">1967–1975: California governorship</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Governorship_of_Ronald_Reagan" title="Governorship of Ronald Reagan">Governorship of Ronald Reagan</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Ronald_Reagan_and_Nancy_Reagan_at_airport,_1972.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="The Reagans at an airport, 1972" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d6/Ronald_Reagan_and_Nancy_Reagan_at_airport%2C_1972.jpg/220px-Ronald_Reagan_and_Nancy_Reagan_at_airport%2C_1972.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="237" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d6/Ronald_Reagan_and_Nancy_Reagan_at_airport%2C_1972.jpg/330px-Ronald_Reagan_and_Nancy_Reagan_at_airport%2C_1972.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d6/Ronald_Reagan_and_Nancy_Reagan_at_airport%2C_1972.jpg/440px-Ronald_Reagan_and_Nancy_Reagan_at_airport%2C_1972.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2394" data-file-height="2577" /></a><figcaption>The Reagans in 1972</figcaption></figure>
<p>Brown had spent much of California's funds on new programs, prompting them to use <a href="/wiki/Accrual_accounting" class="mw-redirect" title="Accrual accounting">accrual accounting</a> to avoid raising taxes. Consequently, it generated a larger deficit,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon20035_110-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon20035-110">&#91;110&#93;</a></sup> and Reagan would call for reduced government spending and tax hikes to <a href="/wiki/Balance_the_budget" class="mw-redirect" title="Balance the budget">balance the budget</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard201264_111-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard201264-111">&#91;111&#93;</a></sup> He worked with <a href="/wiki/Jesse_M._Unruh" title="Jesse M. Unruh">Jesse M. Unruh</a> on securing tax increases and promising future property tax cuts. This caused some conservatives to accuse Reagan of betraying his principles.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015157–159_112-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015157–159-112">&#91;112&#93;</a></sup> As a result, taxes on sales, banks, corporate profits, inheritances, liquor, and cigarettes jumped. <a href="/wiki/Kevin_Starr" title="Kevin Starr">Kevin Starr</a> states, Reagan "gave Californians the biggest tax hike in their history—and got away with it."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPutnam200626_113-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPutnam200626-113">&#91;113&#93;</a></sup> In <a href="/wiki/1970_California_gubernatorial_election" title="1970 California gubernatorial election">the 1970 gubernatorial election</a>, Unruh used Reagan's tax policy against him, saying it disproportionally favored the wealthy. Reagan countered that he was still committed to reducing property taxes.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESchuparra201547–48_114-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchuparra201547–48-114">&#91;114&#93;</a></sup> By 1973, the budget had a surplus, which Reagan preferred "to give back to the people".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2003370_115-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2003370-115">&#91;115&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 1967, Reagan reacted to the <a href="/wiki/Black_Panther_Party" title="Black Panther Party">Black Panther Party</a>'s strategy of <a href="/wiki/Copwatch" title="Copwatch">copwatching</a> by signing the <a href="/wiki/Mulford_Act" title="Mulford Act">Mulford Act</a><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHayesFortunatoHibbing2020819_116-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHayesFortunatoHibbing2020819-116">&#91;116&#93;</a></sup> to prohibit the public carrying of firearms. The act was California's most restrictive piece of <a href="/wiki/Gun_politics_in_the_United_States" title="Gun politics in the United States">gun control legislation</a>, with critics saying that it was "overreacting to the political activism of organizations such as the Black Panthers".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECarter2002493_117-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarter2002493-117">&#91;117&#93;</a></sup> The act marked the beginning of both modern legislation and <a href="/wiki/Public_opinion_on_gun_control_in_the_United_States" title="Public opinion on gun control in the United States">public attitude studies</a> on gun control.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHayesFortunatoHibbing2020819_116-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHayesFortunatoHibbing2020819-116">&#91;116&#93;</a></sup> Reagan also signed the 1967 Therapeutic Abortion Act that allowed abortions in the cases of rape and incest when a doctor determined the birth would impair the physical or mental health of the mother. He later expressed regret over signing it, saying that he was unaware of the mental health provision. He believed that doctors were interpreting the provision loosely and more abortions were resulting.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2003209–214_118-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2003209–214-118">&#91;118&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>After Reagan won the 1966 election, he and his advisors planned a run in the <a href="/wiki/1968_Republican_Party_presidential_primaries" title="1968 Republican Party presidential primaries">1968 Republican presidential primaries</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton199876_119-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton199876-119">&#91;119&#93;</a></sup> He ran as an unofficial candidate to cut into Nixon's southern support and be a compromise candidate if there were to be a <a href="/wiki/Brokered_convention" title="Brokered convention">brokered convention</a>. He won California's delegates,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGould201092–93_120-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGould201092–93-120">&#91;120&#93;</a></sup> but Nixon secured enough delegates for <a href="/wiki/1968_Republican_National_Convention" title="1968 Republican National Convention">the nomination</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGould201096–97_121-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGould201096–97-121">&#91;121&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Reagan had previously been critical of former governor Brown and university administrators for tolerating student demonstrations in the city of <a href="/wiki/Berkeley,_California" title="Berkeley, California">Berkeley</a>, making it a major theme in his campaigning.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2003271_122-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2003271-122">&#91;122&#93;</a></sup> 
On February 5, 1969, Reagan declared a state of emergency in response to ongoing protests and acts of violence at the University of California, Berkeley, and sent in the <a href="/wiki/California_Highway_Patrol" title="California Highway Patrol">California Highway Patrol</a>. In May 1969, these officers, along with local officers from Berkeley and Alameda county, <a href="/wiki/1969_People%27s_Park_protest" title="1969 People&#39;s Park protest">clashed with protestors</a> over a site known as <a href="/wiki/People%27s_Park_(Berkeley)" title="People&#39;s Park (Berkeley)">the People's Park</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2003291–292_123-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2003291–292-123">&#91;123&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-124" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-124">&#91;124&#93;</a></sup> One student was shot and killed while many police officers and two reporters were injured. Reagan then commanded the <a href="/wiki/California_National_Guard" title="California National Guard">state National Guard troops</a> to occupy Berkeley for seventeen days to subdue the protesters, allowing other students to attend class safely. In February 1970, violent protests broke out near the <a href="/wiki/University_of_California,_Santa_Barbara" title="University of California, Santa Barbara">University of California, Santa Barbara</a>, where he once again deployed the National Guard. On April 7, Reagan defended his policies regarding campus protests, saying, "If it takes a bloodbath, let's get it over with. No more appeasement."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2003295_125-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2003295-125">&#91;125&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>During his victorious reelection campaign in 1970, Reagan, remaining critical of government, promised to prioritize <a href="/wiki/Welfare_reform" title="Welfare reform">welfare reform</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard201273,_75_126-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard201273,_75-126">&#91;126&#93;</a></sup> He was concerned that the programs were disincentivizing work and that the growing welfare rolls would lead to both an unbalanced budget and another big tax hike in 1972.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard201275_127-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard201275-127">&#91;127&#93;</a></sup> At the same time, the <a href="/wiki/Federal_Reserve" title="Federal Reserve">Federal Reserve</a> increased interest rates to combat inflation, putting the American economy in <a href="/wiki/Recession_of_1969%E2%80%931970" title="Recession of 1969–1970">a mild recession</a>. Reagan worked with <a href="/wiki/Bob_Moretti" title="Bob Moretti">Bob Moretti</a> to tighten up the eligibility requirements so that the financially needy could continue receiving payments. This was only accomplished after Reagan softened his criticism of Nixon's <a href="/wiki/Family_Assistance_Plan" title="Family Assistance Plan">Family Assistance Plan</a>. Nixon then lifted regulations to shepherd California's experiment.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015179–181_128-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015179–181-128">&#91;128&#93;</a></sup> In 1976, the <a href="/wiki/Employment_Development_Department" title="Employment Development Department">Employment Development Department</a> published a report suggesting that the experiment that ran from 1971 to 1974 was unsuccessful.<sup id="cite_ref-129" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-129">&#91;129&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Reagan did not run for the governorship <a href="/wiki/1974_California_gubernatorial_election" title="1974 California gubernatorial election">in 1974</a> and it was won by Pat Brown's son, <a href="/wiki/Jerry_Brown" title="Jerry Brown">Jerry</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2000754–755_130-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2000754–755-130">&#91;130&#93;</a></sup> Reagan's governorship, as professor Gary K. Clabaugh writes, saw public schools deteriorate due to his opposition to additional basic education funding.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEClabaugh2004257_131-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClabaugh2004257-131">&#91;131&#93;</a></sup> As for higher education, journalist William Trombley believed that the budget cuts Reagan enacted damaged Berkeley's student-faculty ratio and research.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2003296_132-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2003296-132">&#91;132&#93;</a></sup> Additionally, the homicide rate doubled and armed robbery rates rose as well during Reagan's eight years, even with the many laws Reagan signed to try toughening criminal sentencing and reforming the criminal justice system.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2003388_133-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2003388-133">&#91;133&#93;</a></sup> Reagan strongly supported capital punishment, but his efforts to enforce it were thwarted by <i><a href="/wiki/People_v._Anderson" title="People v. Anderson">People v. Anderson</a></i> in 1972.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2003223–224_134-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2003223–224-134">&#91;134&#93;</a></sup> According to his son, Michael, Reagan said that he regretted signing the Family Law Act that granted <a href="/wiki/No-fault_divorce" title="No-fault divorce">no-fault divorces</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReagan201167_135-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReagan201167-135">&#91;135&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span id="1975.E2.80.931981:_Seeking_the_presidency"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="1975–1981:_Seeking_the_presidency">1975–1981: Seeking the presidency</span></h2>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="1976_Republican_primaries">1976 Republican primaries</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Ronald_Reagan_1976_presidential_campaign" title="Ronald Reagan 1976 presidential campaign">Ronald Reagan 1976 presidential campaign</a> and <a href="/wiki/1976_Republican_Party_presidential_primaries" title="1976 Republican Party presidential primaries">1976 Republican Party presidential primaries</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:1976_Republican_National_Convention.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Reagan and Gerald Ford shaking hands on the podium after Reagan narrowly lost the nomination at the 1976 Republican National Convention" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/1976_Republican_National_Convention.jpg/220px-1976_Republican_National_Convention.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="150" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/1976_Republican_National_Convention.jpg/330px-1976_Republican_National_Convention.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/1976_Republican_National_Convention.jpg/440px-1976_Republican_National_Convention.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4497" data-file-height="3059" /></a><figcaption>Reagan and Gerald Ford shaking hands on the podium after Reagan narrowly lost the nomination at the <a href="/wiki/1976_Republican_National_Convention" title="1976 Republican National Convention">1976 Republican National Convention</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>Insufficiently conservative to Reagan<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard201278_136-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard201278-136">&#91;136&#93;</a></sup> and many other Republicans,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPrimuth201645_137-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrimuth201645-137">&#91;137&#93;</a></sup> president <a href="/wiki/Gerald_Ford" title="Gerald Ford">Gerald Ford</a> suffered from multiple political and economic woes. Ford, running for president, was disappointed to hear him also run.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard201284–87_138-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard201284–87-138">&#91;138&#93;</a></sup> Reagan was strongly critical of <a href="/wiki/D%C3%A9tente" title="Détente">détente</a> and Ford's policy of détente with the Soviet Union.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKengor200648_139-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKengor200648-139">&#91;139&#93;</a></sup> He repeated "A Time for Choosing" around the country<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015193–194_140-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015193–194-140">&#91;140&#93;</a></sup> before announcing his campaign on November 20, 1975, when he discussed economic and social problems, and to a lesser extent, foreign affairs.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPrimuth201647_141-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrimuth201647-141">&#91;141&#93;</a></sup> Both candidates were determined to knock each other out early in the primaries,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWitcover1977433_142-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWitcover1977433-142">&#91;142&#93;</a></sup> but Reagan would devastatingly lose the first five primaries beginning with New Hampshire,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard201289–90_143-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard201289–90-143">&#91;143&#93;</a></sup> where he popularized the <a href="/wiki/Welfare_queen" title="Welfare queen">welfare queen</a> narrative about <a href="/wiki/Linda_Taylor" title="Linda Taylor">Linda Taylor</a>, exaggerating her misuse of welfare benefits and igniting voter resentment for welfare reform,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBoris2007612–613_144-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBoris2007612–613-144">&#91;144&#93;</a></sup> but never overtly mentioning her name or race.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2000457_145-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2000457-145">&#91;145&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In Florida, Reagan referred to a "strapping young buck",<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPrimuth201648_146-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrimuth201648-146">&#91;146&#93;</a></sup> which became an example of <a href="/wiki/Dog_whistle_politics" class="mw-redirect" title="Dog whistle politics">dog whistle politics</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHaney_López20144_147-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHaney_López20144-147">&#91;147&#93;</a></sup> and accused Ford for handing the <a href="/wiki/Panama_Canal" title="Panama Canal">Panama Canal</a> to Panama's government while Ford implied that he would <a href="/wiki/Social_Security_debate_in_the_United_States" title="Social Security debate in the United States">end Social Security</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard201289–90_143-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard201289–90-143">&#91;143&#93;</a></sup> Then, in Illinois, he again criticized Ford's policy and his secretary of state, <a href="/wiki/Henry_Kissinger" title="Henry Kissinger">Henry Kissinger</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWitcover1977404_148-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWitcover1977404-148">&#91;148&#93;</a></sup> Losing the first five primaries prompted Reagan to desperately win North Carolina's by running a grassroots campaign and uniting with the <a href="/wiki/Jesse_Helms" title="Jesse Helms">Jesse Helms</a> political machine that viciously attacked Ford. Reagan won an upset victory, convincing party delegates that Ford's nomination was no longer guaranteed.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard201291Primuth201648_149-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard201291Primuth201648-149">&#91;149&#93;</a></sup> Reagan won subsequent victories in Texas, Alabama, Georgia, and Indiana with his attacks on social programs, opposition to <a href="/wiki/Forced_busing" class="mw-redirect" title="Forced busing">forced busing</a>, increased support from inclined voters of a declining <a href="/wiki/George_Wallace" title="George Wallace">George Wallace</a> presidential campaign,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPrimuth201649–50_150-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrimuth201649–50-150">&#91;150&#93;</a></sup> and repeated criticisms of Ford and Kissinger's policies, including détente.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPatterson2005104_151-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPatterson2005104-151">&#91;151&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The result was a seesaw battle for the 1,130 delegates required for their party's nomination that neither would reach before the <a href="/wiki/1976_Republican_National_Convention" title="1976 Republican National Convention">Kansas City convention</a><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard201292–93_152-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard201292–93-152">&#91;152&#93;</a></sup> in August<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBoller2004345_153-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBoller2004345-153">&#91;153&#93;</a></sup> and Ford replacing mentions of détente with Reagan's preferred phrase, "<a href="/wiki/Peace_through_strength" title="Peace through strength">peace through strength</a>".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKengor200649_154-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKengor200649-154">&#91;154&#93;</a></sup> Reagan took <a href="/wiki/John_Sears_(political_strategist)" title="John Sears (political strategist)">John Sears</a>' advice of choosing liberal <a href="/wiki/Richard_Schweiker" title="Richard Schweiker">Richard Schweiker</a> as his running mate, hoping to pry loose of delegates from Pennsylvania and other states,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015204_155-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015204-155">&#91;155&#93;</a></sup> and distract Ford. Instead, conservatives were left alienated, and Ford picked up the remaining uncommitted delegates and prevailed, earning 1,187 to Reagan's 1,070. Before giving his acceptance speech, Ford invited Reagan to address the convention; Reagan emphasized individual freedom<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard201293–94_156-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard201293–94-156">&#91;156&#93;</a></sup> and the dangers of nuclear weapons. In 1977, Ford told Cannon that Reagan's primary challenge contributed to his own narrow loss to Democrat <a href="/wiki/Jimmy_Carter" title="Jimmy Carter">Jimmy Carter</a> in the <a href="/wiki/1976_United_States_presidential_election" title="1976 United States presidential election">1976 United States presidential election</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2003432,_434_157-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2003432,_434-157">&#91;157&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="1980_election">1980 election</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Ronald_Reagan_1980_presidential_campaign" title="Ronald Reagan 1980 presidential campaign">Ronald Reagan 1980 presidential campaign</a> and <a href="/wiki/1980_United_States_presidential_election" title="1980 United States presidential election">1980 United States presidential election</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:ElectoralCollege1980.svg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Results for the 1980 United States presidential election" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5c/ElectoralCollege1980.svg/290px-ElectoralCollege1980.svg.png" decoding="async" width="290" height="169" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5c/ElectoralCollege1980.svg/435px-ElectoralCollege1980.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5c/ElectoralCollege1980.svg/580px-ElectoralCollege1980.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="1020" data-file-height="593" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/1980_United_States_presidential_election" title="1980 United States presidential election">1980 United States presidential election</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>Reagan emerged as a vocal critic of President Carter in 1977. The <a href="/wiki/Panama_Canal_Treaty" class="mw-redirect" title="Panama Canal Treaty">Panama Canal Treaty</a>'s signing, the <a href="/wiki/1979_oil_crisis" title="1979 oil crisis">1979 oil crisis</a>, and rise in the inflation, interest and unemployment rates helped set up his 1980 presidential campaign,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard201299–101_158-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard201299–101-158">&#91;158&#93;</a></sup> which he announced on November 13, 1979<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton199886_159-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton199886-159">&#91;159&#93;</a></sup> with an indictment of the federal government.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard2012102_160-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard2012102-160">&#91;160&#93;</a></sup> His announcement stressed his fundamental principles of tax cuts to stimulate the economy and having both a <a href="/wiki/Small_government" class="mw-redirect" title="Small government">small government</a> and a strong <a href="/wiki/National_defense" class="mw-redirect" title="National defense">national defense</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton199886–87_161-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton199886–87-161">&#91;161&#93;</a></sup> since he believed the United States was behind the Soviet Union militarily.<sup id="cite_ref-Bowman_2004_162-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Bowman_2004-162">&#91;162&#93;</a></sup> Heading into 1980, his age became an issue among the press, and the United States was in <a href="/wiki/Early_1980s_recession" title="Early 1980s recession">a severe recession</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard2012102–103_163-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard2012102–103-163">&#91;163&#93;</a></sup> In <a href="/wiki/1980_Republican_Party_presidential_primaries" title="1980 Republican Party presidential primaries">the primaries</a>, Reagan unexpectedly lost the Iowa caucus to <a href="/wiki/George_H._W._Bush" title="George H. W. Bush">George H. W. Bush</a>. Three days before the New Hampshire primary, the Reagan and Bush campaigns agreed to a one-on-one debate sponsored by <i><a href="/wiki/The_Telegraph_(Nashua,_New_Hampshire)" title="The Telegraph (Nashua, New Hampshire)">The Telegraph</a></i> at <a href="/wiki/Nashua,_New_Hampshire" title="Nashua, New Hampshire">Nashua, New Hampshire</a>, but hours before the debate, the Reagan campaign invited other candidates including <a href="/wiki/Bob_Dole" title="Bob Dole">Bob Dole</a>, <a href="/wiki/John_B._Anderson" title="John B. Anderson">John B. Anderson</a>, <a href="/wiki/Howard_Baker" title="Howard Baker">Howard Baker</a> and <a href="/wiki/Phil_Crane" title="Phil Crane">Phil Crane</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-164" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-164">&#91;164&#93;</a></sup> Debate moderator Jon Breen denied seats to the other candidates, asserting that <i>The Telegraph</i> would violate federal campaign contribution laws if it sponsored the debate and changed the ground rules hours before the debate.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBirkner1987283–289_165-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBirkner1987283–289-165">&#91;165&#93;</a></sup> As a result, the Reagan campaign agreed to pay for the debate. Reagan said that as he was funding the debate, he could decide who would debate.<sup id="cite_ref-166" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-166">&#91;166&#93;</a></sup> During the debate, when Breen was laying out the ground rules and attempting to ask the first question, Reagan interrupted in protest to make an introductory statement and wanted other candidates to be included before the debate began.<sup id="cite_ref-167" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-167">&#91;167&#93;</a></sup> The moderator asked Bob Malloy, the volume operator, to mute Reagan's microphone. After Malloy repeated his demand to Malloy, Reagan furiously replied, "I am paying for this microphone, Mr. Green! [sic]".<sup id="cite_ref-169" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-169">&#91;a&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-170" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-170">&#91;169&#93;</a></sup> This turned out to be the turning point of the debate and the primary race.<sup id="cite_ref-171" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-171">&#91;170&#93;</a></sup> Ultimately, the four additional candidates left, and the debate continued between Reagan and Bush. Reagan's polling numbers improved, and he won the New Hampshire primary by more than 39,000 votes.<sup id="cite_ref-172" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-172">&#91;171&#93;</a></sup> Soon thereafter, Reagan's opponents began dropping out of the primaries, including Anderson, who left the party to become an independent candidate. Reagan easily captured the presidential nomination and chose Bush as his running mate at the <a href="/wiki/1980_Republican_National_Convention" title="1980 Republican National Convention">Detroit convention</a> in July.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton199887–89_173-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton199887–89-173">&#91;172&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The general election pitted Reagan against Carter amid the multitude of domestic concerns and ongoing <a href="/wiki/Iran_hostage_crisis" title="Iran hostage crisis">Iran hostage crisis</a> that began on November 4, 1979.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton199889–90Woodard2012101_174-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton199889–90Woodard2012101-174">&#91;173&#93;</a></sup> Reagan's campaign worried that Carter would be able to secure the release of the American hostages in Iran as part of the <a href="/wiki/October_surprise" title="October surprise">October surprise</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard2012110_175-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard2012110-175">&#91;174&#93;</a></sup> Carter "suggested that Reagan would wreck Social Security" and portrayed him as a warmonger,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon200183–84_176-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon200183–84-176">&#91;175&#93;</a></sup> and Anderson carried support <a href="/wiki/Rockefeller_Republican" title="Rockefeller Republican">from liberal Republicans</a> dissatisfied with Reagan's conservatism.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard2012110_175-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard2012110-175">&#91;174&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-178" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-178">&#91;b&#93;</a></sup> One of Reagan's key strengths was his appeal to the rising conservative movement. Though most conservative leaders espoused cutting taxes and budget deficits, many conservatives focused more closely on social issues like abortion and homosexuality.<sup id="cite_ref-179" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-179">&#91;177&#93;</a></sup> Evangelical Protestants became an increasingly important voting bloc, and they generally supported Reagan.<sup id="cite_ref-180" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-180">&#91;178&#93;</a></sup> Reagan also won the backing of <a href="/wiki/Reagan_Democrat" title="Reagan Democrat">Reagan Democrats</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-181" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-181">&#91;179&#93;</a></sup> Though he advocated socially conservative view points, Reagan focused much of his campaign on attacks against Carter's foreign policy.<sup id="cite_ref-182" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-182">&#91;180&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In August, Reagan gave <a href="/wiki/States%27_rights_speech" title="States&#39; rights speech">a speech at the Neshoba County Fair</a>, stating his belief in <a href="/wiki/States%27_rights" title="States&#39; rights">states' rights</a>. <a href="/wiki/Joseph_Crespino" title="Joseph Crespino">Joseph Crespino</a> argues that the visit was designed to reach out to Wallace-inclined voters,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECrespino20211_183-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrespino20211-183">&#91;181&#93;</a></sup> and some also saw these actions as an extension of the <a href="/wiki/Southern_strategy" title="Southern strategy">Southern strategy</a> to garner white support for Republican candidates.<sup id="cite_ref-184" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-184">&#91;182&#93;</a></sup> Reagan's supporters have said that this was his typical anti-big government rhetoric, without racial context or intent.<sup id="cite_ref-185" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-185">&#91;183&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBennettLivingston2021279_186-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBennettLivingston2021279-186">&#91;184&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-187" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-187">&#91;185&#93;</a></sup> In the <a href="/wiki/1980_United_States_presidential_debates" title="1980 United States presidential debates">October 28 debate</a>, Carter chided Reagan for being against national health insurance. Reagan replied, "<a href="/wiki/There_you_go_again" title="There you go again">There you go again</a>", though the audience laughed and viewers found him more appealing.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015228–229_188-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015228–229-188">&#91;186&#93;</a></sup> Reagan later asked the audience if they were better off than they were four years ago, slightly paraphrasing Roosevelt's words in 1934.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon200183_189-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon200183-189">&#91;187&#93;</a></sup> In 1983, Reagan's campaign managers were revealed to having <a href="/wiki/Debategate" title="Debategate">obtained Carter's debate briefing book</a> before the debates.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBoller2004368_190-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBoller2004368-190">&#91;188&#93;</a></sup> On November 4, 1980, Reagan won in a decisive victory in the Electoral College over Carter, carrying 44 states and receiving 489 electoral votes to Carter's 49 in six states and the District of Columbia. He won the popular vote by a narrower margin, receiving nearly 51 percent to Carter's 41 percent and Anderson's 7 percent. In the <a href="/wiki/United_States_Congress" title="United States Congress">United States Congress</a>, Republicans <a href="/wiki/1980_United_States_Senate_elections" title="1980 United States Senate elections">won a majority of seats in the Senate</a> for the first time since 1952<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon200187_191-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon200187-191">&#91;189&#93;</a></sup> while Democrats <a href="/wiki/1980_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections" title="1980 United States House of Representatives elections">retained the House of Representatives</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2000755_192-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2000755-192">&#91;190&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span id="1981.E2.80.931989:_Presidency"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="1981–1989:_Presidency">1981–1989: Presidency</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Presidency_of_Ronald_Reagan" title="Presidency of Ronald Reagan">Presidency of Ronald Reagan</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">For a chronological guide, see <a href="/wiki/Timeline_of_the_Ronald_Reagan_presidency" title="Timeline of the Ronald Reagan presidency">Timeline of the Ronald Reagan presidency</a>.</div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/Domestic_policy_of_the_Ronald_Reagan_administration" title="Domestic policy of the Ronald Reagan administration">Domestic policy of the Ronald Reagan administration</a> and <a href="/wiki/Foreign_policy_of_the_Ronald_Reagan_administration" title="Foreign policy of the Ronald Reagan administration">Foreign policy of the Ronald Reagan administration</a></div>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="First_inauguration">First inauguration</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/First_inauguration_of_Ronald_Reagan" title="First inauguration of Ronald Reagan">First inauguration of Ronald Reagan</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:President_Ronald_Reagan_making_his_inaugural_address_from_the_United_States_Capitol.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Reagan giving his inauguration speech at the United States Captiol, 1981" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/15/President_Ronald_Reagan_making_his_inaugural_address_from_the_United_States_Capitol.jpg/220px-President_Ronald_Reagan_making_his_inaugural_address_from_the_United_States_Capitol.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="146" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/15/President_Ronald_Reagan_making_his_inaugural_address_from_the_United_States_Capitol.jpg/330px-President_Ronald_Reagan_making_his_inaugural_address_from_the_United_States_Capitol.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/15/President_Ronald_Reagan_making_his_inaugural_address_from_the_United_States_Capitol.jpg/440px-President_Ronald_Reagan_making_his_inaugural_address_from_the_United_States_Capitol.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3000" data-file-height="1996" /></a><figcaption>Reagan delivering his inaugural address, 1981</figcaption></figure>
<p>The 40th president of the United States,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard2012xiv_193-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard2012xiv-193">&#91;191&#93;</a></sup> Reagan was sworn into office for his first term on January 20, 1981. In his <a href="https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/en:Ronald_Reagan%27s_First_Inaugural_Address" class="extiw" title="s:en:Ronald Reagan&#39;s First Inaugural Address">inaugural address</a>, he addressed the country's economic malaise, arguing, "In this present crisis, government is not the solution to our problem, government is the problem."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard2012116–117_194-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard2012116–117-194">&#91;192&#93;</a></sup> In a final insult to President Carter, Iran had waited until Reagan had been sworn in before sending the hostages home.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPatterson2005126_195-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPatterson2005126-195">&#91;193&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span id=".22Reaganomics.22_and_the_economy"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="&quot;Reaganomics&quot;_and_the_economy">"Reaganomics" and the economy</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Reaganomics" title="Reaganomics">Reaganomics</a></div>
<p>Reagan advocated a <i><a href="/wiki/Laissez-faire" title="Laissez-faire">laissez-faire</a></i> philosophy,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKaraagac2002113_196-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaraagac2002113-196">&#91;194&#93;</a></sup> and promoted a set of <a href="/wiki/Neoliberal" class="mw-redirect" title="Neoliberal">neoliberal</a> reforms dubbed "Reaganomics", which included <a href="/wiki/Monetarism" title="Monetarism">monetarism</a> and <a href="/wiki/Supply-side_economics" title="Supply-side economics">supply-side economics</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTELi2013221Gerstle2022150Roy2012155_197-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTELi2013221Gerstle2022150Roy2012155-197">&#91;195&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Taxation">Taxation</span></h4>

srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/6/6c/Wiki_letter_w.svg/66px-Wiki_letter_w.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/6/6c/Wiki_letter_w.svg/88px-Wiki_letter_w.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="44" data-file-height="44" /></a></span></div></td><td class="mbox-text"><div class="mbox-text-span">This section <b>is missing information</b> about analysis.<span class="hide-when-compact"> Please expand the section to include this information. Further details may exist on the <a href="/wiki/Talk:Ronald_Reagan" title="Talk:Ronald Reagan">talk page</a>.</span>  <span class="date-container"><i>(<span class="date">April 2023</span>)</i></span></div></td></tr></tbody></table>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:President_Ronald_Reagan_addresses_the_nation_from_the_Oval_Office_on_tax_reduction_legislation.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Reagan addressing the nation from the Oval Office on tax reduction legislation, 1981" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/President_Ronald_Reagan_addresses_the_nation_from_the_Oval_Office_on_tax_reduction_legislation.jpg/220px-President_Ronald_Reagan_addresses_the_nation_from_the_Oval_Office_on_tax_reduction_legislation.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="145" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/President_Ronald_Reagan_addresses_the_nation_from_the_Oval_Office_on_tax_reduction_legislation.jpg/330px-President_Ronald_Reagan_addresses_the_nation_from_the_Oval_Office_on_tax_reduction_legislation.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/President_Ronald_Reagan_addresses_the_nation_from_the_Oval_Office_on_tax_reduction_legislation.jpg/440px-President_Ronald_Reagan_addresses_the_nation_from_the_Oval_Office_on_tax_reduction_legislation.jpg 2x" data-file-width="6600" data-file-height="4361" /></a><figcaption>Reagan outlining his plan for tax cuts, 1981</figcaption></figure>
<p>Reagan worked with the <a href="/wiki/Boll_weevil_Democrats" class="mw-redirect" title="Boll weevil Democrats">boll weevil Democrats</a> to pass tax and budget legislation in a Congress led by <a href="/wiki/Tip_O%27Neill" title="Tip O&#39;Neill">Tip O'Neill</a>, a liberal who strongly criticized Reaganomics.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2001100Pemberton199899–102_198-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2001100Pemberton199899–102-198">&#91;196&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-200" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-200">&#91;c&#93;</a></sup> He lifted federal oil and gasoline price controls on January 28, 1981,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGraetz201234_201-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGraetz201234-201">&#91;198&#93;</a></sup> and in August, he signed the <a href="/wiki/Economic_Recovery_Tax_Act_of_1981" title="Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981">Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981</a><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998103_202-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998103-202">&#91;199&#93;</a></sup> to dramatically lower federal <a href="/wiki/Income_tax_in_the_United_States" title="Income tax in the United States">income tax rates</a> and require exemptions and brackets to be indexed for inflation starting in 1985.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESteuerle199242_203-0" class="reference"><a
