href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESteuerle199242-203">&#91;200&#93;</a></sup> Amid growing concerns about <a href="/wiki/National_debt_of_the_United_States" title="National debt of the United States">the mounting federal debt</a>, Reagan signed the <a href="/wiki/Tax_Equity_and_Fiscal_Responsibility_Act_of_1982" title="Tax Equity and Fiscal Responsibility Act of 1982">Tax Equity and Fiscal Responsibility Act of 1982</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998127–128_204-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998127–128-204">&#91;201&#93;</a></sup> one of the eleven times Reagan raised taxes.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBartlett201244_205-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBartlett201244-205">&#91;202&#93;</a></sup> The bill doubled <a href="/wiki/Cigarette_taxes_in_the_United_States" title="Cigarette taxes in the United States">the federal cigarette tax</a>, rescinded a portion of the corporate tax cuts from the 1981 tax bill,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTERossinow201562_206-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTERossinow201562-206">&#91;203&#93;</a></sup> and according to <a href="/wiki/Paul_Krugman" title="Paul Krugman">Paul Krugman</a>, "a third of the 1981 cut" overall.<sup id="cite_ref-207" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-207">&#91;204&#93;</a></sup> Many of his supporters condemned the bill, but Reagan defended his preservation of cuts on individual income tax rates.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998128_208-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998128-208">&#91;205&#93;</a></sup> By 1983, the amount of federal tax had fallen for all or most taxpayers, but most strongly affected the wealthy.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTERossinow201563_209-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTERossinow201563-209">&#91;206&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The <a href="/wiki/Tax_Reform_Act_of_1986" title="Tax Reform Act of 1986">Tax Reform Act of 1986</a> reduced the number of tax brackets and top tax rate, and almost doubled <a href="/wiki/Personal_exemption" title="Personal exemption">personal exemptions</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998145_210-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998145-210">&#91;207&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>To Reagan, <a href="/wiki/Reagan_tax_cuts" title="Reagan tax cuts">the tax cuts</a> would not have increased the deficit as long as there was enough economic growth and spending cuts. His policies proposed that economic growth would occur when the tax cuts spur investments, which would result in more spending, consumption, and ergo tax revenue. This theoretical relationship has been illustrated by some with the controversial <a href="/wiki/Laffer_curve" title="Laffer curve">Laffer curve</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton199896Woodard2012119_211-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton199896Woodard2012119-211">&#91;208&#93;</a></sup> Critics labeled this "<a href="/wiki/Trickle-down_economics" title="Trickle-down economics">trickle-down economics</a>", the belief that tax policies that benefit the wealthy will spread to the poor.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2000222_212-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2000222-212">&#91;209&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Milton_Friedman" title="Milton Friedman">Milton Friedman</a> and <a href="/wiki/Robert_Mundell" title="Robert Mundell">Robert Mundell</a> argued that these policies invigorated America's economy and contributed to the <a href="/wiki/1990s_United_States_boom" title="1990s United States boom">economic boom of the 1990s</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-213" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-213">&#91;210&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Inflation_and_unemployment">Inflation and unemployment</span></h4>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:1981%E2%80%931989_monthly_unemployment,_inflation,_and_interest_rates.svg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Line charts showing Bureau of Labor Statistics and Federal Reserve Economic Data information on the monthly unemployment, inflation, and interest rates from January 1981 to January 1989" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/08/1981%E2%80%931989_monthly_unemployment%2C_inflation%2C_and_interest_rates.svg/290px-1981%E2%80%931989_monthly_unemployment%2C_inflation%2C_and_interest_rates.svg.png" decoding="async" width="290" height="218" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/08/1981%E2%80%931989_monthly_unemployment%2C_inflation%2C_and_interest_rates.svg/435px-1981%E2%80%931989_monthly_unemployment%2C_inflation%2C_and_interest_rates.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/08/1981%E2%80%931989_monthly_unemployment%2C_inflation%2C_and_interest_rates.svg/580px-1981%E2%80%931989_monthly_unemployment%2C_inflation%2C_and_interest_rates.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="1000" data-file-height="750" /></a><figcaption>Monthly unemployment, inflation, and interest rates from January 1981 to January 1989 according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics and <a href="/wiki/Federal_Reserve_Economic_Data" title="Federal Reserve Economic Data">Federal Reserve Economic Data</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>Reagan took office in the midst of <a href="/wiki/Stagflation" title="Stagflation">stagflation</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTELi2013221_214-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTELi2013221-214">&#91;211&#93;</a></sup> The economy briefly experienced growth before plunging into a recession in July 1981.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTERossinow201590_215-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTERossinow201590-215">&#91;212&#93;</a></sup> As Federal Reserve chairman, <a href="/wiki/Paul_Volcker" title="Paul Volcker">Paul Volcker</a> fought inflation by pursuing <a href="/wiki/Shock_therapy_(economics)" title="Shock therapy (economics)">a tight money policy of high interest rates</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015318_216-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015318-216">&#91;213&#93;</a></sup> which restricted lending and investment, raised unemployment, and temporarily reduced economic growth.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTERossinow201589–90_217-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTERossinow201589–90-217">&#91;214&#93;</a></sup> In December 1982, the <a href="/wiki/Bureau_of_Labor_Statistics" title="Bureau of Labor Statistics">Bureau of Labor Statistics</a> (BLS) measured the unemployment rate at 10.8 percent.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDeGrasse198314_218-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeGrasse198314-218">&#91;215&#93;</a></sup> Around the same time, economic activity <a href="/wiki/List_of_economic_expansions_in_the_United_States" title="List of economic expansions in the United States">began to rise until its end in 1990</a>, setting the record for the longest peacetime expansion.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESinai19921_219-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESinai19921-219">&#91;216&#93;</a></sup> In 1983, the recession ended<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015452_220-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015452-220">&#91;217&#93;</a></sup> and Reagan nominated Volcker to a second term in fear of damaging confidence in the economic recovery.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015668_221-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015668-221">&#91;218&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Reagan appointed <a href="/wiki/Alan_Greenspan" title="Alan Greenspan">Alan Greenspan</a> to succeed Volcker in 1987. Greenspan raised interest rates in another attempt to curb inflation, setting off <a href="/wiki/Black_Monday_(1987)" title="Black Monday (1987)">the Black Monday</a> although the markets eventually recovered.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015669–671_222-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015669–671-222">&#91;219&#93;</a></sup> By 1989, the BLS measured the unemployment rate at 5.3 percent.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTELi2013219_223-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTELi2013219-223">&#91;220&#93;</a></sup> The inflation rate dropped from 12 percent during the 1980 election to under 5 percent in 1989. Likewise, the interest rate dropped from 15 percent to under 10 percent.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998206_224-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998206-224">&#91;221&#93;</a></sup> Yet, not all shared equally in the economic recovery, and both <a href="/wiki/Income_inequality_in_the_United_States" title="Income inequality in the United States">economic inequality</a><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPatterson2005166–167_225-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPatterson2005166–167-225">&#91;222&#93;</a></sup> and the number of <a href="/wiki/Homelessness_in_the_United_States" title="Homelessness in the United States">homeless individuals</a> increased during the 1980s.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTERossinow2015144–145_226-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTERossinow2015144–145-226">&#91;223&#93;</a></sup> Critics have contended that a majority of the jobs created during this decade paid the minimum wage.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998207_227-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998207-227">&#91;224&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Government_spending">Government spending</span></h4>
<p>In 1981, in an effort to keep it solvent, Reagan approved a plan for cuts <a href="/wiki/Social_Security_(United_States)" title="Social Security (United States)">to Social Security</a>. He later backed off of these plans due to public backlash.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015300–303_228-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015300–303-228">&#91;225&#93;</a></sup> He then created the <a href="/wiki/Greenspan_Commission" title="Greenspan Commission">Greenspan Commission</a> to keep Social Security financially secure and in 1983, he signed amendments to raise both the program's payroll taxes and retirement age for benefits.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPatterson2005163–164_229-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPatterson2005163–164-229">&#91;226&#93;</a></sup> He had signed the <a href="/wiki/Omnibus_Budget_Reconciliation_Act_of_1981" title="Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1981">Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1981</a> to cut funding for <a href="/wiki/Federal_assistance" class="mw-redirect" title="Federal assistance">federal assistance</a> such as food stamps, <a href="/wiki/Unemployment_benefits" title="Unemployment benefits">unemployment benefits</a>, <a href="/wiki/Subsidized_housing" title="Subsidized housing">subsidized housing</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Aid_to_Families_with_Dependent_Children" title="Aid to Families with Dependent Children">Aid to Families with Dependent Children</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998141_230-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998141-230">&#91;227&#93;</a></sup> and would discontinue the <a href="/wiki/Comprehensive_Employment_and_Training_Act" title="Comprehensive Employment and Training Act">Comprehensive Employment and Training Act</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPatterson2005157_231-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPatterson2005157-231">&#91;228&#93;</a></sup> On the other side, defense spending doubled between 1981 and 1985.<sup id="cite_ref-Bowman_2004_162-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Bowman_2004-162">&#91;162&#93;</a></sup> During Reagan's presidency, <a href="/wiki/Project_Socrates" title="Project Socrates">Project Socrates</a> operated within the <a href="/wiki/Defense_Intelligence_Agency" title="Defense Intelligence Agency">Defense Intelligence Agency</a> to discover why the United States was unable to maintain its economic competitiveness. According to program director Michael Sekora, their findings helped the country exceed Soviet missile defense technology.<sup id="cite_ref-232" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-232">&#91;229&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFialka19998_233-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFialka19998-233">&#91;230&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Deregulation">Deregulation</span></h4>
<p>Reagan sought to loosen federal regulation of economic activities, and he appointed key officials who shared this agenda. <a href="/wiki/William_Leuchtenburg" title="William Leuchtenburg">William Leuchtenburg</a> writes that by 1986, the Reagan administration eliminated almost half of the federal regulations that had existed in 1981.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTELeuchtenburg2015602–604_234-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeuchtenburg2015602–604-234">&#91;231&#93;</a></sup> The 1982 <a href="/wiki/Garn%E2%80%93St._Germain_Depository_Institutions_Act" title="Garn–St. Germain Depository Institutions Act">Garn–St. Germain Depository Institutions Act</a> deregulated <a href="/wiki/Savings_and_loan_association" title="Savings and loan association">savings and loan associations</a> by letting them make a variety of loans and investments outside of real estate.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998130_235-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998130-235">&#91;232&#93;</a></sup> After the bill's passage, savings and loans associations engaged in riskier activities, and the leaders of some institutions embezzled funds. The administration's inattentiveness toward the industry contributed to the <a href="/wiki/Savings_and_loan_crisis" title="Savings and loan crisis">savings and loan crisis</a> and costly bailouts.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPatterson2005175_236-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPatterson2005175-236">&#91;233&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Deficits">Deficits</span></h4>
<p>The deficits were exacerbated by the early 1980s recession, which cut into federal revenue.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTELeuchtenburg2015605–606_237-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeuchtenburg2015605–606-237">&#91;234&#93;</a></sup> The national debt tripled between the fiscal years of 1980 and 1989, and the national debt as a percentage of the gross domestic product rose from 33 percent in 1981 to 53 percent by 1989. During his time in office, Reagan never fulfilled his 1980 campaign promise of submitting a <a href="/wiki/Balanced_budget" title="Balanced budget">balanced budget</a>. The United States borrowed heavily to cover newly spawned federal budget deficits.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPatterson2005158–159Woodard2012132_238-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPatterson2005158–159Woodard2012132-238">&#91;235&#93;</a></sup> Reagan described the tripled debt the "greatest disappointment of his presidency".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2001128_239-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2001128-239">&#91;236&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Jeffrey_Frankel" title="Jeffrey Frankel">Jeffrey Frankel</a> opined that the deficits were a major reason why Reagan's successor, Bush, reneged on <a href="/wiki/Read_my_lips:_no_new_taxes" title="Read my lips: no new taxes">his campaign promise</a> by raising taxes through the <a href="/wiki/Budget_Enforcement_Act_of_1990" title="Budget Enforcement Act of 1990">Budget Enforcement Act of 1990</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-240" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-240">&#91;237&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Assassination_attempt">Assassination attempt</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Attempted_assassination_of_Ronald_Reagan" title="Attempted assassination of Ronald Reagan">Attempted assassination of Ronald Reagan</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:President_Ronald_Reagan_moments_before_he_was_shot_in_an_assassination_attempt_1981.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Ronald Reagan waves his hand as he walks out of the Washington Hilton. Surrounding him are secret service agents, policemen, press secretary James Brady, and aide Michael Deaver." src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d5/President_Ronald_Reagan_moments_before_he_was_shot_in_an_assassination_attempt_1981.jpg/220px-President_Ronald_Reagan_moments_before_he_was_shot_in_an_assassination_attempt_1981.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="146" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d5/President_Ronald_Reagan_moments_before_he_was_shot_in_an_assassination_attempt_1981.jpg/330px-President_Ronald_Reagan_moments_before_he_was_shot_in_an_assassination_attempt_1981.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d5/President_Ronald_Reagan_moments_before_he_was_shot_in_an_assassination_attempt_1981.jpg/440px-President_Ronald_Reagan_moments_before_he_was_shot_in_an_assassination_attempt_1981.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3000" data-file-height="1993" /></a><figcaption>Reagan moments before he was shot, 1981</figcaption></figure>
<p>On March 30, 1981, Reagan was shot by <a href="/wiki/John_Hinckley_Jr." title="John Hinckley Jr.">John Hinckley Jr.</a> outside the <a href="/wiki/Washington_Hilton" title="Washington Hilton">Washington Hilton</a>. Also struck were: <a href="/wiki/James_Brady" title="James Brady">James Brady</a>, <a href="/wiki/Thomas_Delahanty" title="Thomas Delahanty">Thomas Delahanty</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Tim_McCarthy" title="Tim McCarthy">Tim McCarthy</a>. Although "right on the margin of death" upon arrival at <a href="/wiki/George_Washington_University_Hospital" title="George Washington University Hospital">George Washington University Hospital</a>, Reagan underwent surgery and recovered quickly from a broken rib, a punctured lung, and internal bleeding. Professor J. David Woodard says that the assassination attempt "created a bond between him and the American people that was never really broken".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard2012120–123_241-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard2012120–123-241">&#91;238&#93;</a></sup> Later, Reagan came to believe that God had spared his life "for a chosen mission".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKengor2004210_242-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKengor2004210-242">&#91;239&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Supreme_Court_appointments">Supreme Court appointments</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Ronald_Reagan_Supreme_Court_candidates" title="Ronald Reagan Supreme Court candidates">Ronald Reagan Supreme Court candidates</a></div>
<p>Reagan appointed three Associate Justices to the <a href="/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States" title="Supreme Court of the United States">Supreme Court of the United States</a>: <a href="/wiki/Sandra_Day_O%27Connor" title="Sandra Day O&#39;Connor">Sandra Day O'Connor</a> in 1981, <a href="/wiki/Antonin_Scalia" title="Antonin Scalia">Antonin Scalia</a> in 1986, and <a href="/wiki/Anthony_Kennedy" title="Anthony Kennedy">Anthony Kennedy</a> in 1988. He also elevated <a href="/wiki/William_Rehnquist" title="William Rehnquist">William Rehnquist</a> from Associate Justice to Chief Justice in 1986.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998147–148_243-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998147–148-243">&#91;240&#93;</a></sup> The direction of the Supreme Court's reshaping has been described as conservative.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEShull199344_244-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShull199344-244">&#91;241&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998148_245-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998148-245">&#91;242&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Public_sector_labor_union_fights">Public sector labor union fights</span></h3>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:President_Ronald_Reagan_making_a_statement_to_the_press_regarding_the_air_traffic_controllers_strike.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Ronald Reagan speaks to the press in the Rose Garden about the Professional Air Traffic Controllers Organization strike." src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/President_Ronald_Reagan_making_a_statement_to_the_press_regarding_the_air_traffic_controllers_strike.jpg/220px-President_Ronald_Reagan_making_a_statement_to_the_press_regarding_the_air_traffic_controllers_strike.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/President_Ronald_Reagan_making_a_statement_to_the_press_regarding_the_air_traffic_controllers_strike.jpg/330px-President_Ronald_Reagan_making_a_statement_to_the_press_regarding_the_air_traffic_controllers_strike.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/President_Ronald_Reagan_making_a_statement_to_the_press_regarding_the_air_traffic_controllers_strike.jpg/440px-President_Ronald_Reagan_making_a_statement_to_the_press_regarding_the_air_traffic_controllers_strike.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4000" data-file-height="2671" /></a><figcaption>Reagan making a statement to the press regarding the air traffic controllers strike, 1981</figcaption></figure>
<p>Early in August 1981, the <a href="/wiki/Professional_Air_Traffic_Controllers_Organization_(1968)" title="Professional Air Traffic Controllers Organization (1968)">Professional Air Traffic Controllers Organization</a> (PATCO) went on strike, violating a federal law prohibiting government unions from striking.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTERossinow201585–86_246-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTERossinow201585–86-246">&#91;243&#93;</a></sup> On August 3, Reagan said that he would fire air traffic controllers if they did not return to work within 48 hours; according to him, 38 percent did not return. On August 13, Reagan fired roughly 12,000 striking air traffic controllers who ignored his order.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998107_247-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998107-247">&#91;244&#93;</a></sup> He used military controllers<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPatterson2005158_248-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPatterson2005158-248">&#91;245&#93;</a></sup> and supervisors to handle the nation's commercial air traffic until new controllers could be hired and trained.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTERossinow201586_249-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTERossinow201586-249">&#91;246&#93;</a></sup> The breaking of the PATCO strike demoralized organized labor, and the number of strikes fell greatly in the 1980s.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPatterson2005158_248-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPatterson2005158-248">&#91;245&#93;</a></sup> With the assent of Reagan's sympathetic <a href="/wiki/National_Labor_Relations_Board" title="National Labor Relations Board">National Labor Relations Board</a> appointees, many companies also won wage and benefit cutbacks from unions, especially in the manufacturing sector.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTERossinow201588_250-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTERossinow201588-250">&#91;247&#93;</a></sup> During Reagan's presidency, the share of employees who were part of a labor union dropped from approximately one-fourth of the total workforce to approximately one-sixth of the total workforce.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPatterson2005170_251-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPatterson2005170-251">&#91;248&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Civil_rights">Civil rights</span></h3>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:President_Ronald_Reagan_at_the_Signing_Ceremony_for_Martin_Luther_King_Holiday_Legislation.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Ronald Reagan at the signing ceremony for Martin Luther King Jr. Day legislation in the Rose Garden. Coretta Scott King, George H. W. Bush, Howard Baker, Bob Dole, Jack Kemp, Samuel Pierce, and Katie Hall looking on." src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/President_Ronald_Reagan_at_the_Signing_Ceremony_for_Martin_Luther_King_Holiday_Legislation.jpg/220px-President_Ronald_Reagan_at_the_Signing_Ceremony_for_Martin_Luther_King_Holiday_Legislation.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="146" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/President_Ronald_Reagan_at_the_Signing_Ceremony_for_Martin_Luther_King_Holiday_Legislation.jpg/330px-President_Ronald_Reagan_at_the_Signing_Ceremony_for_Martin_Luther_King_Holiday_Legislation.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/President_Ronald_Reagan_at_the_Signing_Ceremony_for_Martin_Luther_King_Holiday_Legislation.jpg/440px-President_Ronald_Reagan_at_the_Signing_Ceremony_for_Martin_Luther_King_Holiday_Legislation.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3150" data-file-height="2088" /></a><figcaption>Reagan signing the Passage of Martin Luther King Jr. Day, 1983</figcaption></figure>
<p>Despite Reagan having opposed the <a href="/wiki/Voting_Rights_Act_of_1965" title="Voting Rights Act of 1965">Voting Rights Act of 1965</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2000458_31-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2000458-31">&#91;31&#93;</a></sup> the bill was extended for 25 years in 1982.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKeyssar2009213_252-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKeyssar2009213-252">&#91;249&#93;</a></sup> He initially opposed the establishment of <a href="/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr._Day" title="Martin Luther King Jr. Day">Martin Luther King Jr. Day</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-253" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-253">&#91;250&#93;</a></sup> but signed <a href="/wiki/Passage_of_Martin_Luther_King_Jr._Day" title="Passage of Martin Luther King Jr. Day">a veto-proof bill to create the holiday in 1983</a>, and also alluded to <a href="/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr.#Allegations_of_communism" title="Martin Luther King Jr.">claims that King was associated with communists</a> during his career.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2000461_254-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2000461-254">&#91;251&#93;</a></sup> In 1984, he signed legislation intended to impose fines for <a href="/wiki/Fair_housing" class="mw-redirect" title="Fair housing">fair housing</a> discrimination offenses.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEShull199356–57_255-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShull199356–57-255">&#91;252&#93;</a></sup> In March 1988, Reagan vetoed the <a href="/wiki/Civil_Rights_Restoration_Act_of_1987" title="Civil Rights Restoration Act of 1987">Civil Rights Restoration Act of 1987</a>, but Congress overrode his veto. He had argued that the bill unreasonably increased the federal government's power and undermined the rights of churches and business owners.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2000462–463_256-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2000462–463-256">&#91;253&#93;</a></sup> Later in September, legislation was passed to correct loopholes in the <a href="/wiki/Fair_Housing_Act_of_1968" class="mw-redirect" title="Fair Housing Act of 1968">Fair Housing Act of 1968</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-257" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-257">&#91;254&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEShull199314_258-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShull199314-258">&#91;255&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Early in his presidency, Reagan appointed <a href="/wiki/Clarence_M._Pendleton_Jr." title="Clarence M. Pendleton Jr.">Clarence M. Pendleton Jr.</a> as chair of the <a href="/wiki/United_States_Commission_on_Civil_Rights" title="United States Commission on Civil Rights">United States Commission on Civil Rights</a> to criticism for politicizing the agency. Pendleton and Reagan's subsequent appointees steered the commission in line with Reagan's views on civil rights, arousing the ire of civil rights advocates.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEShull1993114–116_259-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShull1993114–116-259">&#91;256&#93;</a></sup> In 1987, Reagan unsuccessfully <a href="/wiki/Robert_Bork_Supreme_Court_nomination" title="Robert Bork Supreme Court nomination">nominated Robert Bork</a> to the Supreme Court as a way to achieve his civil rights policy that could not be fulfilled during his presidency; his administration had opposed <a href="/wiki/Affirmative_action" title="Affirmative action">affirmative action</a>, particularly in education, federal assistance programs, housing and employment,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEAmaker1988157–159_260-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAmaker1988157–159-260">&#91;257&#93;</a></sup> but Reagan reluctantly continued these policies.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPatterson2005171_261-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPatterson2005171-261">&#91;258&#93;</a></sup> In housing, Reagan's administration saw considerably fewer fair housing cases filed than the three previous administrations.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEAmaker198892–95_262-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAmaker198892–95-262">&#91;259&#93;</a></sup> Reagan's recasting of civil rights through reduced enforcement of civil rights laws has been regarded by some as the largest since <a href="/wiki/Lyndon_B._Johnson%27s_presidency" class="mw-redirect" title="Lyndon B. Johnson&#39;s presidency">Lyndon B. Johnson's presidency</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEShull19933–4Reimler199938_263-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShull19933–4Reimler199938-263">&#91;260&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="War_on_drugs">War on drugs</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/War_on_drugs" title="War on drugs">War on drugs</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:President_Ronald_Reagan_signing_the_Anti_Drug_Abuse_Act_of_1986.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Ronald Reagan with Nancy Reagan, Paula Hawkins, Charles Rangel and Benjamin Gilman for the signing ceremony for the Anti-Drug Abuse Act of 1986 in the East Room, 1986" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/57/President_Ronald_Reagan_signing_the_Anti_Drug_Abuse_Act_of_1986.jpg/220px-President_Ronald_Reagan_signing_the_Anti_Drug_Abuse_Act_of_1986.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="145" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/57/President_Ronald_Reagan_signing_the_Anti_Drug_Abuse_Act_of_1986.jpg/330px-President_Ronald_Reagan_signing_the_Anti_Drug_Abuse_Act_of_1986.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/57/President_Ronald_Reagan_signing_the_Anti_Drug_Abuse_Act_of_1986.jpg/440px-President_Ronald_Reagan_signing_the_Anti_Drug_Abuse_Act_of_1986.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4000" data-file-height="2638" /></a><figcaption>Reagan signing the Anti-Drug Abuse Act of 1986</figcaption></figure>
<p>In response to concerns about the increasing <a href="/wiki/Crack_epidemic" class="mw-redirect" title="Crack epidemic">crack epidemic</a>, Reagan intensified the war on drugs in 1982.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEAlexander20105_264-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander20105-264">&#91;261&#93;</a></sup> While the American public did not see drugs as an important issue then, the FBI, <a href="/wiki/Drug_Enforcement_Administration" title="Drug Enforcement Administration">Drug Enforcement Administration</a> and the <a href="/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense" title="United States Department of Defense">United States Department of Defense</a> all increased their <a href="/wiki/Anti-drug" class="mw-redirect" title="Anti-drug">anti-drug</a> funding immensely.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEAlexander201049_265-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander201049-265">&#91;262&#93;</a></sup> Reagan's administration publicized the campaign to gain support after crack became widespread in 1985.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEAlexander201052_266-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander201052-266">&#91;263&#93;</a></sup> Reagan signed the <a href="/wiki/Anti-Drug_Abuse_Act_of_1986" title="Anti-Drug Abuse Act of 1986">Anti-Drug Abuse Act of 1986</a> and <a href="/wiki/Anti-Drug_Abuse_Act_of_1988" title="Anti-Drug Abuse Act of 1988">1988</a> to specify penalties for drug offenses.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEAlexander201053_267-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAlexander201053-267">&#91;264&#93;</a></sup> Both bills have been criticized in the years since for promoting <a href="/wiki/Race_and_the_war_on_drugs" title="Race and the war on drugs">racial disparities</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESirin201191–96_268-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESirin201191–96-268">&#91;265&#93;</a></sup> Additionally, Nancy Reagan founded the "<a href="/wiki/Just_Say_No" title="Just Say No">Just Say No</a>" campaign to discourage others from engaging in <a href="/wiki/Recreational_drug_use" title="Recreational drug use">recreational drug use</a> and raise awareness about the dangers of drugs.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard2012163–164_269-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard2012163–164-269">&#91;266&#93;</a></sup> A 1988 study showed 39 percent of high school seniors using illegal drugs compared to 53 percent in 1980,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon200010_270-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon200010-270">&#91;267&#93;</a></sup> but <a href="/wiki/Scott_Lilienfeld" title="Scott Lilienfeld">Scott Lilienfeld</a> and Hal Arkowitz say that the success of these types of campaigns have not been found to be affirmatively proven.<sup id="cite_ref-271" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-271">&#91;268&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Escalation_of_the_Cold_War">Escalation of the Cold War</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/Cold_War_(1979%E2%80%931985)" title="Cold War (1979–1985)">Cold War (1979–1985)</a> and <a href="/wiki/Reagan_Doctrine" title="Reagan Doctrine">Reagan Doctrine</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Reagan_sitting_with_people_from_the_Afghanistan-Pakistan_region_in_February_1983.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Reagan in the Oval Office, sitting with people from the Afghanistan-Pakistan region, February 1983" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/Reagan_sitting_with_people_from_the_Afghanistan-Pakistan_region_in_February_1983.jpg/220px-Reagan_sitting_with_people_from_the_Afghanistan-Pakistan_region_in_February_1983.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="155" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/Reagan_sitting_with_people_from_the_Afghanistan-Pakistan_region_in_February_1983.jpg/330px-Reagan_sitting_with_people_from_the_Afghanistan-Pakistan_region_in_February_1983.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/Reagan_sitting_with_people_from_the_Afghanistan-Pakistan_region_in_February_1983.jpg/440px-Reagan_sitting_with_people_from_the_Afghanistan-Pakistan_region_in_February_1983.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2707" data-file-height="1911" /></a><figcaption>Reagan meeting with <a href="/wiki/Afghan_mujahideen" class="mw-redirect" title="Afghan mujahideen">Afghan mujahideen</a> leaders in the <a href="/wiki/Oval_Office" title="Oval Office">Oval Office</a>, 1983</figcaption></figure>
<p>Reagan ordered a massive defense buildup;<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton19984_272-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton19984-272">&#91;269&#93;</a></sup> he revived the <a href="/wiki/B-1_Lancer" class="mw-redirect" title="B-1 Lancer">B-1 Lancer</a> program that had been rejected by the <a href="/wiki/Carter_administration" class="mw-redirect" title="Carter administration">Carter administration</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHerring2008868_273-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHerring2008868-273">&#91;270&#93;</a></sup> and deployed the <a href="/wiki/MX_missile" class="mw-redirect" title="MX missile">MX missile</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon200037_274-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon200037-274">&#91;271&#93;</a></sup> In response to Soviet deployment of the <a href="/wiki/SS-20" class="mw-redirect" title="SS-20">SS-20</a>, he oversaw <a href="/wiki/NATO" title="NATO">NATO</a>'s deployment of the <a href="/wiki/Pershing_missile" class="mw-redirect" title="Pershing missile">Pershing missile</a> in Western Europe.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2000260_275-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2000260-275">&#91;272&#93;</a></sup> In 1982, Reagan tried to cut off the Soviet Union's access to <a href="/wiki/Hard_currency" title="Hard currency">hard currency</a> by impeding its proposed gas line to Western Europe. It hurt the Soviet economy, but it also caused much ill will among American allies in Europe who counted on that revenue; he later retreated on this issue.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGraebnerBurnsSiracusa200829–31_276-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGraebnerBurnsSiracusa200829–31-276">&#91;273&#93;</a></sup> In March 1983, Reagan introduced the <a href="/wiki/Strategic_Defense_Initiative" title="Strategic Defense Initiative">Strategic Defense Initiative</a> (SDI) to protect the United States from space intercontinental ballistic missiles. He believed that this defense shield could protect the country from nuclear destruction in a hypothetical nuclear war with the Soviet Union.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998131_277-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998131-277">&#91;274&#93;</a></sup> There was much disbelief among the scientific community surrounding the program's scientific feasibility, leading opponents to dub the SDI "Star Wars",<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015418_278-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015418-278">&#91;275&#93;</a></sup> though Soviet leader <a href="/wiki/Yuri_Andropov" title="Yuri Andropov">Yuri Andropov</a> said it would lead to "an extremely dangerous path".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998132_279-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998132-279">&#91;276&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:President_Ronald_Reagan_in_Meeting_with_President_Mohammad_Zia_Ul_Haq_of_Pakistan_in_Oval_Office.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/President_Ronald_Reagan_in_Meeting_with_President_Mohammad_Zia_Ul_Haq_of_Pakistan_in_Oval_Office.jpg/220px-President_Ronald_Reagan_in_Meeting_with_President_Mohammad_Zia_Ul_Haq_of_Pakistan_in_Oval_Office.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="145" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/President_Ronald_Reagan_in_Meeting_with_President_Mohammad_Zia_Ul_Haq_of_Pakistan_in_Oval_Office.jpg/330px-President_Ronald_Reagan_in_Meeting_with_President_Mohammad_Zia_Ul_Haq_of_Pakistan_in_Oval_Office.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/President_Ronald_Reagan_in_Meeting_with_President_Mohammad_Zia_Ul_Haq_of_Pakistan_in_Oval_Office.jpg/440px-President_Ronald_Reagan_in_Meeting_with_President_Mohammad_Zia_Ul_Haq_of_Pakistan_in_Oval_Office.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4000" data-file-height="2642" /></a><figcaption>Reagan listening to Pakistani president <a href="/wiki/Muhammad_Zia-ul-Haq" title="Muhammad Zia-ul-Haq">Muhammad Zia-ul-Haq</a>, 1982</figcaption></figure>
<p>In a 1982 address to the <a href="/wiki/British_Parliament" class="mw-redirect" title="British Parliament">British Parliament</a>, Reagan said, "the march of freedom and democracy&#160;... will leave <a href="/wiki/Marxism%E2%80%93Leninism" title="Marxism–Leninism">Marxism–Leninism</a> on the <a href="/wiki/Ash_heap_of_history" title="Ash heap of history">ash heap of history</a>." Dismissed by the American press as "wishful thinking", <a href="/wiki/Margaret_Thatcher" title="Margaret Thatcher">Margaret Thatcher</a> called the address a "triumph".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2000271–272_280-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2000271–272-280">&#91;277&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/David_Cannadine" title="David Cannadine">David Cannadine</a> says of Thatcher that "Reagan had been grateful for her interest in him at a time when the British establishment refused to take him seriously" with the two agreeing on "building up stronger defenses against Soviet Russia" and both believing in outfacing "what Reagan would later call '<a href="/wiki/Evil_Empire_speech" title="Evil Empire speech">the evil empire</a>'"<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannadine201738_281-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannadine201738-281">&#91;278&#93;</a></sup> in reference to the Soviet Union during a speech to the <a href="/wiki/National_Association_of_Evangelicals" title="National Association of Evangelicals">National Association of Evangelicals</a> in March 1983.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998130_235-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998130-235">&#91;232&#93;</a></sup> After Soviet fighters downed <a href="/wiki/Korean_Air_Lines_Flight_007" title="Korean Air Lines Flight 007">Korean Air Lines Flight 007</a> in September, which included <a href="/wiki/Larry_McDonald" title="Larry McDonald">Larry McDonald</a> and 61 other Americans, Reagan expressed outrage towards the Soviet Union.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015420–421_282-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015420–421-282">&#91;279&#93;</a></sup> The next day, reports suggested that the Soviets had fired on the plane by mistake.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998133_283-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998133-283">&#91;280&#93;</a></sup> In spite of the harsh, discordant rhetoric,<sup id="cite_ref-284" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-284">&#91;281&#93;</a></sup> Reagan's administration continued discussions with the Soviet Union on <a href="/wiki/START_I" title="START I">START I</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHerring2008868–869_285-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHerring2008868–869-285">&#91;282&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Although the Reagan administration agreed with the communist government in China to <a href="/wiki/Three_Communiqu%C3%A9s" title="Three Communiqués">reduce the sale of arms to Taiwan</a> in 1982,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2000270_286-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2000270-286">&#91;283&#93;</a></sup> Reagan himself was the first president to reject <a href="/wiki/Containment" title="Containment">containment</a> and détente, and to put into practice the concept that the Soviet Union could be defeated rather than simply negotiated with.<sup id="cite_ref-Knopf_287-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Knopf-287">&#91;284&#93;</a></sup> His <a href="/wiki/Operation_Cyclone" title="Operation Cyclone">covert aid</a> to <a href="/wiki/Afghan_mujahideen" class="mw-redirect" title="Afghan mujahideen">Afghan mujahideen</a> forces through Pakistan against the Soviets has been given credit for assisting in ending the <a href="/wiki/Soviet_occupation_of_Afghanistan" class="mw-redirect" title="Soviet occupation of Afghanistan">Soviet occupation of Afghanistan</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBergen200168_288-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBergen200168-288">&#91;285&#93;</a></sup> However, the United States was subjected <a href="/wiki/Blowback_(intelligence)" title="Blowback (intelligence)">to blowback</a> in the form of the <a href="/wiki/Taliban" title="Taliban">Taliban</a> that opposed them in <a href="/wiki/War_in_Afghanistan_(2001%E2%80%932021)" title="War in Afghanistan (2001–2021)">the war in Afghanistan</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHerring2008883–884_289-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHerring2008883–884-289">&#91;286&#93;</a></sup> In his <a href="/wiki/1985_State_of_the_Union_Address" title="1985 State of the Union Address">1985 State of the Union Address</a>, Reagan proclaimed, "Support for freedom fighters is self-defense."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2000320_290-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2000320-290">&#91;287&#93;</a></sup> Through the <a href="/wiki/Reagan_Doctrine" title="Reagan Doctrine">Reagan Doctrine</a>, his administration supported <a href="/wiki/Anti-communist" class="mw-redirect" title="Anti-communist">anti-communist</a> movements that fought against groups backed by the Soviet Union in an effort to <a href="/wiki/Rollback" title="Rollback">rollback</a> Soviet-backed communist governments and reduce Soviet influence across the world.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKanet2006340Pach200678_291-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKanet2006340Pach200678-291">&#91;288&#93;</a></sup> Critics have felt that the administration ignored the <a href="/wiki/Human_rights_violations" class="mw-redirect" title="Human rights violations">human rights violations</a> in the countries they backed,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWawro2010381Søndergaard20204_292-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWawro2010381Søndergaard20204-292">&#91;289&#93;</a></sup> including <a href="/wiki/Guatemalan_genocide#Genocide_under_Ríos_Montt" title="Guatemalan genocide">genocide in Guatemala</a><sup id="cite_ref-293" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-293">&#91;290&#93;</a></sup> and mass killings in Chad.<sup id="cite_ref-294" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-294">&#91;291&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Invasion_of_Grenada">Invasion of Grenada</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/United_States_invasion_of_Grenada" title="United States invasion of Grenada">United States invasion of Grenada</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:President_Ronald_Reagan_discusses_the_situation_in_Grenada_with_a_group_of_bipartisan_members_of_Congress.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Reagan in the White House to discuss the Grenada situation with a bipartisan group of members of Congress, October 1983" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/75/President_Ronald_Reagan_discusses_the_situation_in_Grenada_with_a_group_of_bipartisan_members_of_Congress.jpg/220px-President_Ronald_Reagan_discusses_the_situation_in_Grenada_with_a_group_of_bipartisan_members_of_Congress.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="146" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/75/President_Ronald_Reagan_discusses_the_situation_in_Grenada_with_a_group_of_bipartisan_members_of_Congress.jpg/330px-President_Ronald_Reagan_discusses_the_situation_in_Grenada_with_a_group_of_bipartisan_members_of_Congress.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/75/President_Ronald_Reagan_discusses_the_situation_in_Grenada_with_a_group_of_bipartisan_members_of_Congress.jpg/440px-President_Ronald_Reagan_discusses_the_situation_in_Grenada_with_a_group_of_bipartisan_members_of_Congress.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4000" data-file-height="2656" /></a><figcaption>Reagan discussing the Grenada situation with a bipartisan group of members of Congress, 1983</figcaption></figure>
<p>On October 19, 1983, <a href="/wiki/Maurice_Bishop" title="Maurice Bishop">Maurice Bishop</a> was overthrown and murdered by one of his colleagues. Several days later, Reagan ordered American forces to invade Grenada. Reagan cited a regional threat posed by a Soviet-Cuban military build-up in the Caribbean nation and concern for the safety of hundreds of American medical students at <a href="/wiki/St._George%27s_University" title="St. George&#39;s University">St. George's University</a> as adequate reasons to invade. Two days of fighting commenced, resulting in an American victory.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2001187–188_295-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2001187–188-295">&#91;292&#93;</a></sup> While the invasion enjoyed public support in the United States, it was criticized internationally, with the <a href="/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly" title="United Nations General Assembly">United Nations General Assembly</a> voting to censure the American government.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015403_296-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015403-296">&#91;293&#93;</a></sup> Cannon later noted that throughout Reagan's 1984 presidential campaign, the invasion overshadowed the <a href="/wiki/1983_Beirut_barracks_bombings" title="1983 Beirut barracks bombings">1983 Beirut barracks bombings</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2000393_297-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2000393-297">&#91;294&#93;</a></sup> which killed 241 Americans taking part in <a href="/wiki/Multinational_Force_in_Lebanon" title="Multinational Force in Lebanon">an international peacekeeping operation</a> during the <a href="/wiki/Lebanese_Civil_War" title="Lebanese Civil War">Lebanese Civil War</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTELawrence2021176_298-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTELawrence2021176-298">&#91;295&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="1984_election">1984 election</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Ronald_Reagan_1984_presidential_campaign" title="Ronald Reagan 1984 presidential campaign">Ronald Reagan 1984 presidential campaign</a> and <a href="/wiki/1984_United_States_presidential_election" title="1984 United States presidential election">1984 United States presidential election</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:ElectoralCollege1984.svg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Results for the 1984 United States presidential election" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ab/ElectoralCollege1984.svg/290px-ElectoralCollege1984.svg.png" decoding="async" width="290" height="169" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ab/ElectoralCollege1984.svg/435px-ElectoralCollege1984.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ab/ElectoralCollege1984.svg/580px-ElectoralCollege1984.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="1020" data-file-height="593" /></a><figcaption>1984 electoral vote results</figcaption></figure>
<p>Reagan announced his reelection campaign on January 29, 1984, declaring, "America is back and standing tall."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998141_230-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998141-230">&#91;227&#93;</a></sup> In February, his administration reversed the unpopular decision to send the <a href="/wiki/United_States_Marine_Corps" title="United States Marine Corps">United States Marine Corps</a> to Lebanon, thus eliminating a political liability for him. Reagan faced minimal opposition in the Republican primaries,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2001188–191_299-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2001188–191-299">&#91;296&#93;</a></sup> and he and Bush accepted the nomination at <a href="/wiki/1984_Republican_National_Convention" title="1984 Republican National Convention">the Dallas convention</a> in August.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBoller2004369_300-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBoller2004369-300">&#91;297&#93;</a></sup> In the general election, his campaign ran the commercial, "<a href="/wiki/Morning_in_America" title="Morning in America">Morning in America</a>".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2000452_301-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2000452-301">&#91;298&#93;</a></sup> At a time when the American economy was already recovering,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015452_220-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015452-220">&#91;217&#93;</a></sup> former vice president <a href="/wiki/Walter_Mondale" title="Walter Mondale">Walter Mondale</a><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015186_302-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015186-302">&#91;299&#93;</a></sup> was attacked by Reagan's campaign as a "tax-and-spend Democrat", while Mondale criticized the deficit, the SDI, and Reagan's civil rights policy. However, Reagan's age induced his campaign managers to minimize his public appearances. Mondale's campaign believed that Reagan's age and mental health were issues before <a href="/wiki/1984_United_States_presidential_debates" title="1984 United States presidential debates">the October presidential debates</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998141–142_303-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998141–142-303">&#91;300&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Following Reagan's performance in the first debate where he struggled to recall statistics, his age was brought up by the media in negative fashion. Reagan's campaign changed his tactics for the second debate where he quipped, "I will not make age an issue of this campaign. I am not going to exploit, for political purposes, my opponent's youth and inexperience." This remark generated applause and laughter,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998142–143_304-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998142–143-304">&#91;301&#93;</a></sup> even from Mondale. At that point, Broder suggested that age was no longer a liability for Reagan,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2001196_305-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2001196-305">&#91;302&#93;</a></sup> and Mondale's campaign felt that "the election was over".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998144_306-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998144-306">&#91;303&#93;</a></sup> In November, Reagan won a landslide reelection victory with 59 percent of the popular vote and 525 electoral votes from 49 states. Mondale won 41 percent of the popular vote and 13 electoral votes from the District of Columbia and his home state of Minnesota.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBoller2004373Cannon2003434_307-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBoller2004373Cannon2003434-307">&#91;304&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Response_to_the_AIDS_epidemic">Response to the AIDS epidemic</span></h3>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:NYC_1987_let_the_record_show.png" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="A 1987 ACT UP art installation quoting Reagan on AIDS with a blank slate to represent silence" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dc/NYC_1987_let_the_record_show.png/190px-NYC_1987_let_the_record_show.png" decoding="async" width="190" height="218" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dc/NYC_1987_let_the_record_show.png/285px-NYC_1987_let_the_record_show.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dc/NYC_1987_let_the_record_show.png/380px-NYC_1987_let_the_record_show.png 2x" data-file-width="400" data-file-height="459" /></a><figcaption>Reagan has been criticized for his delayed and muted response to the AIDS epidemic. This 1987 art installation by <a href="/wiki/ACT_UP" title="ACT UP">ACT UP</a> quotes Reagan on AIDS with a blank slate, representing total silence.</figcaption></figure>
<p>The <a href="/wiki/AIDS_epidemic" class="mw-redirect" title="AIDS epidemic">AIDS epidemic</a> began to unfold in 1981,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGellin199224_308-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGellin199224-308">&#91;305&#93;</a></sup> and AIDS was initially difficult to understand for physicians and the public.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKazanjian2014353_309-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKazanjian2014353-309">&#91;306&#93;</a></sup> As the epidemic advanced, according to White House physician and later physician to the president, brigadier general John Hutton, Reagan thought of AIDS as though "it was the measles and would go away". The October 1985 death of the President's friend <a href="/wiki/Rock_Hudson" title="Rock Hudson">Rock Hudson</a> affected Reagan's view; Reagan approached Hutton for more information on the disease. Still, between September 18, 1985, and February 4, 1986, Reagan did not mention AIDS in public.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2000731_310-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2000731-310">&#91;307&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 1986, Reagan asked <a href="/wiki/C._Everett_Koop" title="C. Everett Koop">C. Everett Koop</a> to draw up a report on the AIDS issue. Koop angered many evangelical conservatives, both in and out of the Reagan administration, by stressing the importance of sex education including condom usage in schools.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2000731–733_311-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2000731–733-311">&#91;308&#93;</a></sup> A year later, Reagan, who reportedly had not read the report,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKoop1991224_312-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKoop1991224-312">&#91;309&#93;</a></sup> gave his first speech on the epidemic when 36,058 Americans had been diagnosed with AIDS, and 20,849 had died of it.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEShilts2000596_313-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShilts2000596-313">&#91;310&#93;</a></sup> Reagan called for increased testing (including routine testing for marriage applicants) and mandatory testing of select groups (including federal prisoners).<sup id="cite_ref-314" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-314">&#91;311&#93;</a></sup> Even after this speech, however, Reagan remained reluctant to publicly address AIDS.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2000chapter_22_315-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2000chapter_22-315">&#91;312&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Scholars and AIDS activists have argued that the Reagan administration largely ignored the <a href="/wiki/AIDS_crisis" class="mw-redirect" title="AIDS crisis">AIDS crisis</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTELucas2009478–479_316-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTELucas2009478–479-316">&#91;313&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFrancis2012290_317-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrancis2012290-317">&#91;314&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKimShin2017518–519_318-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKimShin2017518–519-318">&#91;315&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Randy_Shilts" title="Randy Shilts">Randy Shilts</a> and <a href="/wiki/Michael_Bronski" title="Michael Bronski">Michael Bronski</a> said that AIDS research was chronically underfunded during Reagan's administration, and Bronski added that requests for more funding by doctors at the <a href="/wiki/Centers_for_Disease_Control_and_Prevention" title="Centers for Disease Control and Prevention">Centers for Disease Control and Prevention</a> were routinely denied.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEShilts2000xxii_319-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShilts2000xxii-319">&#91;316&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-320" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-320">&#91;317&#93;</a></sup> In a September 1985 press conference, after Hudson announced his AIDS diagnosis, Reagan called a government AIDS research program a "top priority", but also cited budgetary constraints.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015654,_656_321-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015654,_656-321">&#91;318&#93;</a></sup> Between the fiscal years of 1984 and 1989, federal spending on AIDS totaled $5.6&#160;billion. The Reagan administration proposed $2.8&#160;billion during this time period, but pressure from congressional Democrats resulted in the larger amount.<sup id="cite_ref-322" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-322">&#91;319&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Addressing_apartheid">Addressing apartheid</span></h3>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Reagan_with_Desmond_TutuC26199-10.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Reagan and Desmond Tutu shaking hands in the Oval Office, 1984" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/Reagan_with_Desmond_TutuC26199-10.jpg/220px-Reagan_with_Desmond_TutuC26199-10.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="146" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/Reagan_with_Desmond_TutuC26199-10.jpg/330px-Reagan_with_Desmond_TutuC26199-10.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/Reagan_with_Desmond_TutuC26199-10.jpg/440px-Reagan_with_Desmond_TutuC26199-10.jpg 2x" data-file-width="750" data-file-height="498" /></a><figcaption>Shortly after the 1984 election, Reagan met <a href="/wiki/Desmond_Tutu" title="Desmond Tutu">Desmond Tutu</a>, who described Reagan's administration as "an unmitigated disaster for us blacks",<sup id="cite_ref-323" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-323">&#91;320&#93;</a></sup> and Reagan himself as "a racist pure and simple".<sup id="cite_ref-324" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-324">&#91;321&#93;</a></sup></figcaption></figure>
<p>Opposition to <a href="/wiki/Apartheid" title="Apartheid">apartheid</a> strengthened during Reagan's first term in office as its component <a href="/wiki/Disinvestment_from_South_Africa" title="Disinvestment from South Africa">disinvestment from South Africa</a> movement, which had been in existence for quite some years. The opposition also gained critical mass following in the United States, particularly on college campuses and among <a href="/wiki/Mainline_Protestant" title="Mainline Protestant">mainline Protestant</a> denominations.<sup id="cite_ref-325" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-325">&#91;322&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-326" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-326">&#91;323&#93;</a></sup> President Reagan was opposed to divestiture because, as he wrote in a letter to <a href="/wiki/Sammy_Davis_Jr." title="Sammy Davis Jr.">Sammy Davis Jr.</a>, it "would hurt the very people we are trying to help and would leave us no contact within South Africa to try and bring influence to bear on the government". He also noted the fact that the "American-owned industries there employ more than 80,000 blacks" and that their employment practices were "very different from the normal South African customs".<sup id="cite_ref-327" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-327">&#91;324&#93;</a></sup> The anti-communist focus of Reagan's administration lent itself to closer ties with the apartheid regime of South Africa, particularly with regards to matters pertaining <a href="/wiki/Nuclear_programme_of_South_Africa" title="Nuclear programme of South Africa">to nuclear weapons</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-328" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-328">&#91;325&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The Reagan administration developed <a href="/wiki/Constructive_engagement" title="Constructive engagement">constructive engagement</a><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEThomson2008113_329-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThomson2008113-329">&#91;326&#93;</a></sup> with the South African government as a means of encouraging it to move away from apartheid gradually. It was part of a larger initiative designed to foster peaceful economic development and political change throughout southern Africa.<sup id="cite_ref-AT2008SApolicy_330-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-AT2008SApolicy-330">&#91;327&#93;</a></sup> This policy, however, engendered much public criticism, and renewed calls for the imposition of stringent sanctions.<sup id="cite_ref-UngerVale_331-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-UngerVale-331">&#91;328&#93;</a></sup> In response, Reagan announced the imposition of new sanctions on the South African government, including an <a href="/wiki/Arms_embargo" title="Arms embargo">arms embargo</a> in late 1985.<sup id="cite_ref-332" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-332">&#91;329&#93;</a></sup> These sanctions were seen as weak by anti-apartheid activists and as insufficient by the president's opponents in Congress.<sup id="cite_ref-UngerVale_331-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-UngerVale-331">&#91;328&#93;</a></sup> In 1986, Congress approved the <a href="/wiki/Comprehensive_Anti-Apartheid_Act" title="Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act">Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act</a>, which included tougher sanctions; Reagan's veto was overridden by Congress. Afterward, he remained opposed to apartheid and unsure of "how best to oppose it". Several European countries, as well as Japan, also imposed their sanctions on South Africa soon after.<sup id="cite_ref-333" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-333">&#91;330&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Libya_bombing">Libya bombing</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/1986_United_States_bombing_of_Libya" title="1986 United States bombing of Libya">1986 United States bombing of Libya</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:President_Ronald_Reagan_being_briefed_by_the_National_Security_Council_staff.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Reagan being briefed by the National Security Council Staff on the 1986 Libya air strike in the White House Situation Room. Seated with Reagan is George Shultz, William Casey, Don Regan, and Charles Gabriel." src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/President_Ronald_Reagan_being_briefed_by_the_National_Security_Council_staff.jpg/220px-President_Ronald_Reagan_being_briefed_by_the_National_Security_Council_staff.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="145" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/President_Ronald_Reagan_being_briefed_by_the_National_Security_Council_staff.jpg/330px-President_Ronald_Reagan_being_briefed_by_the_National_Security_Council_staff.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/President_Ronald_Reagan_being_briefed_by_the_National_Security_Council_staff.jpg/440px-President_Ronald_Reagan_being_briefed_by_the_National_Security_Council_staff.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4000" data-file-height="2643" /></a><figcaption>Reagan receiving a briefing on the Libya bombing, 1986</figcaption></figure>
<p>Contentious relations between Libya and the United States under President Reagan were revived in the <a href="/wiki/West_Berlin_discotheque_bombing" title="West Berlin discotheque bombing">West Berlin discotheque bombing</a> that killed an American soldier and injured dozens of others on April 5, 1986. Stating that there was irrefutable evidence that Libya had a direct role in the bombing, Reagan authorized the use of force against the country. On April 14, the United States launched a series of <a href="/wiki/Airstrike" title="Airstrike">airstrikes</a> on ground targets in Libya.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015530–531Woodard2012161_334-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015530–531Woodard2012161-334">&#91;331&#93;</a></sup> Thatcher allowed the <a href="/wiki/United_States_Air_Force" title="United States Air Force">United States Air Force</a> to use Britain's air bases to launch the attack, on the justification that the United Kingdom was supporting America's right to self-defense under Article 51 of the <a href="/wiki/Charter_of_the_United_Nations" title="Charter of the United Nations">Charter of the United Nations</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-335" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-335">&#91;332&#93;</a></sup> The attack was, according to Reagan, designed to halt <a href="/wiki/Muammar_Gaddafi" title="Muammar Gaddafi">Muammar Gaddafi</a>'s "ability to export terrorism", offering him "incentives and reasons to alter his criminal behavior".<sup id="cite_ref-336" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-336">&#91;333&#93;</a></sup> The attack was condemned by many countries; by an overwhelming vote, the United Nations General Assembly adopted a resolution to condemn the attack and deem it a violation of the Charter and international law.<sup id="cite_ref-337" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-337">&#91;334&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span id="Iran.E2.80.93Contra_affair"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Iran–Contra_affair">Iran–Contra affair</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Iran%E2%80%93Contra_affair" title="Iran–Contra affair">Iran–Contra affair</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Photograph_of_President_Reagan_receiving_the_Tower_Commission_Report_in_the_Cabinet_Room_-_NARA_-_198581.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Reagan in the Cabinet Room to receive the Tower Commission Report on the Iran–Contra affair, February 1987" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Photograph_of_President_Reagan_receiving_the_Tower_Commission_Report_in_the_Cabinet_Room_-_NARA_-_198581.jpg/220px-Photograph_of_President_Reagan_receiving_the_Tower_Commission_Report_in_the_Cabinet_Room_-_NARA_-_198581.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="152" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Photograph_of_President_Reagan_receiving_the_Tower_Commission_Report_in_the_Cabinet_Room_-_NARA_-_198581.jpg/330px-Photograph_of_President_Reagan_receiving_the_Tower_Commission_Report_in_the_Cabinet_Room_-_NARA_-_198581.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Photograph_of_President_Reagan_receiving_the_Tower_Commission_Report_in_the_Cabinet_Room_-_NARA_-_198581.jpg/440px-Photograph_of_President_Reagan_receiving_the_Tower_Commission_Report_in_the_Cabinet_Room_-_NARA_-_198581.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3000" data-file-height="2070" /></a><figcaption>Reagan receiving the <a href="/wiki/Tower_Commission_Report" class="mw-redirect" title="Tower Commission Report">Tower Commission Report</a> on the Iran–Contra affair, 1987</figcaption></figure>
<p>Reagan authorized <a href="/wiki/William_J._Casey" title="William J. Casey">William J. Casey</a> to arm the <a href="/wiki/Contras" title="Contras">Contras</a>, fearing that Communists would take over Nicaragua if it remained under the leadership of the <a href="/wiki/Sandinistas" class="mw-redirect" title="Sandinistas">Sandinistas</a>. Congress passed the 1982 <a href="/wiki/Boland_Amendment" title="Boland Amendment">Boland Amendment</a>, prohibiting the CIA and United States Department of Defense from using their budgets to provide aid to the Contras. Still, the Reagan administration raised funds for the Contras from private donors and foreign governments.<sup id="cite_ref-338" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-338">&#91;335&#93;</a></sup> When Congress learned that the CIA had secretly placed <a href="/wiki/Naval_mine" title="Naval mine">naval mines</a> in Nicaraguan harbors, Congress passed a second Boland Amendment that barred granting any assistance to the Contras.<sup id="cite_ref-339" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-339">&#91;336&#93;</a></sup> By mid-1985, <a href="/wiki/Hezbollah" title="Hezbollah">Hezbollah</a> began to <a href="/wiki/Lebanon_hostage_crisis" title="Lebanon hostage crisis">take American hostages in Lebanon</a>, holding seven of them in reaction to the United States' support of Israel.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015488–491_340-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015488–491-340">&#91;337&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Reagan procured the release of seven American hostages held by Hezbollah by selling American arms to Iran, then engaged in the <a href="/wiki/Iran%E2%80%93Iraq_War" title="Iran–Iraq War">Iran–Iraq War</a>, in hopes that Iran would pressure Hezbollah to release the hostages.<sup id="cite_ref-weisberg129134_341-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-weisberg129134-341">&#91;338&#93;</a></sup> The Reagan administration sold over 2,000 missiles to Iran without informing Congress; Hezbollah released four hostages but captured an additional six Americans. On <a href="/wiki/Oliver_North" title="Oliver North">Oliver North</a>'s initiative, the administration redirected the proceeds from the missile sales to the Contras.<sup id="cite_ref-weisberg129134_341-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-weisberg129134-341">&#91;338&#93;</a></sup> The transactions were exposed by <i><a href="/wiki/Ash-Shiraa" title="Ash-Shiraa">Ash-Shiraa</a></i> in early November 1986. Reagan initially denied any wrongdoing, but on November 25, he announced that <a href="/wiki/John_Poindexter" title="John Poindexter">John Poindexter</a> and North had left the administration and that he would form the <a href="/wiki/Tower_Commission" title="Tower Commission">Tower Commission</a> to investigate the transactions. A few weeks later, Reagan asked a panel of federal judges to appoint <a href="/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Justice_Office_of_Special_Counsel" title="United States Department of Justice Office of Special Counsel">a special prosecutor</a> who would conduct a separate investigation.<sup id="cite_ref-342" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-342">&#91;339&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The Tower Commission released a report in February 1987 confirming that the administration had traded arms for hostages and sent the proceeds of the weapons sales to the Contras. The report laid most of the blame on North, Poindexter, and <a href="/wiki/Robert_McFarlane_(American_politician)" class="mw-redirect" title="Robert McFarlane (American politician)">Robert McFarlane</a>, but it was also critical of <a href="/wiki/Donald_Regan" title="Donald Regan">Donald Regan</a> and other White House staffers.<sup id="cite_ref-343" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-343">&#91;340&#93;</a></sup> Investigators did not find conclusive proof that Reagan had known about the aid provided to the Contras, but the report noted that Reagan had "created the conditions which made possible the crimes committed by others" and had "knowingly participated or acquiesced in covering up the scandal".<sup id="cite_ref-344" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-344">&#91;341&#93;</a></sup> The affair damaged the administration and raised questions about Reagan's competency and the wisdom of conservative policies.<sup id="cite_ref-345" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-345">&#91;342&#93;</a></sup> The administration's credibility was also badly damaged on the international stage as it had violated its own arms embargo on Iran.<sup id="cite_ref-346" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-346">&#91;343&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Soviet_decline_and_thaw_in_relations">Soviet decline and thaw in relations</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/Cold_War_(1985%E2%80%931991)" title="Cold War (1985–1991)">Cold War (1985–1991)</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Reagan_and_Gorbachev_signing.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Mikhail Gorbachev and Ronald Reagan signing the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty in the East Room, December 1987" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8d/Reagan_and_Gorbachev_signing.jpg/220px-Reagan_and_Gorbachev_signing.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="136" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8d/Reagan_and_Gorbachev_signing.jpg/330px-Reagan_and_Gorbachev_signing.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8d/Reagan_and_Gorbachev_signing.jpg/440px-Reagan_and_Gorbachev_signing.jpg 2x" data-file-width="5100" data-file-height="3144" /></a><figcaption>Mikhail Gorbachev and Reagan signing the <a href="/wiki/INF_Treaty" class="mw-redirect" title="INF Treaty">INF Treaty</a>, 1987</figcaption></figure>
<p>Although the Soviets did not accelerate military spending in response to Reagan's military buildup,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFischer20198_347-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFischer20198-347">&#91;344&#93;</a></sup> their enormous military expenses, in combination with <a href="/wiki/Collectivization_in_the_Soviet_Union" title="Collectivization in the Soviet Union">collectivized agriculture</a> and inefficient <a href="/wiki/Planned_economy" title="Planned economy">planned manufacturing</a>, were a heavy burden for the <a href="/wiki/Soviet_economy" class="mw-redirect" title="Soviet economy">Soviet economy</a>. At the same time, the prices of oil, the primary source of Soviet export revenues, fell to one third of the previous level in 1985. These factors contributed to a stagnant economy during <a href="/wiki/Mikhail_Gorbachev" title="Mikhail Gorbachev">Mikhail Gorbachev</a>'s tenure as the Soviet Union's leader.<sup id="cite_ref-Gaidar_348-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Gaidar-348">&#91;345&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Reagan's foreign policy towards the Soviets wavered between <a href="/wiki/Brinkmanship" title="Brinkmanship">brinkmanship</a> and cooperation.<sup id="cite_ref-349" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-349">&#91;346&#93;</a></sup> Reagan appreciated Gorbachev's revolutionary change in the direction of the Soviet policy and shifted to diplomacy, intending to encourage him to pursue substantial arms agreements.<sup id="cite_ref-Knopf_287-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Knopf-287">&#91;284&#93;</a></sup> They held <a href="/wiki/List_of_Soviet_Union%E2%80%93United_States_summits#Cold_War_(1985–1991)" title="List of Soviet Union–United States summits">four summit conferences between 1985 and 1988</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-350" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-350">&#91;347&#93;</a></sup> Reagan believed that if he could persuade the Soviets to allow for more democracy and free speech, this would lead to reform and the end of communism.<sup id="cite_ref-351" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-351">&#91;348&#93;</a></sup> The critical summit was in <a href="/wiki/Reykjav%C3%ADk_Summit" title="Reykjavík Summit">Reykjavík in 1986</a>, where they agreed to abolish all nuclear weapons. However, Gorbachev added the condition that SDI research must be confined to laboratories during the ten-year period when disarmament would take place. Reagan refused, stating that it was defensive only and that he would share the secrets with the Soviets, thus failing to reach a deal.<sup id="cite_ref-352" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-352">&#91;349&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In June 1987, Reagan addressed Gorbachev during a speech at the <a href="/wiki/Berlin_Wall" title="Berlin Wall">Berlin Wall</a>, demanding that he "<a href="/wiki/Tear_down_this_wall" class="mw-redirect" title="Tear down this wall">tear down this wall</a>".
