The remark was ignored at the time, but after the wall <a href="/wiki/Fall_of_the_Berlin_Wall" title="Fall of the Berlin Wall">fell in November 1989</a>, it was retroactively recast as a soaring achievement.<sup id="cite_ref-353" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-353">&#91;350&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-354" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-354">&#91;351&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-355" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-355">&#91;352&#93;</a></sup> In December, Reagan and Gorbachev met again at <a href="/wiki/Washington_Summit_(1987)" title="Washington Summit (1987)">the Washington Summit</a><sup id="cite_ref-356" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-356">&#91;353&#93;</a></sup> to sign the <a href="/wiki/Intermediate-Range_Nuclear_Forces_Treaty" title="Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty">Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty</a>, committing to the total abolition of their respective short-range and medium-range missile stockpiles.<sup id="cite_ref-357" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-357">&#91;354&#93;</a></sup> The treaty established an inspections regime designed to ensure that both parties honored the agreement.<sup id="cite_ref-358" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-358">&#91;355&#93;</a></sup> In May 1988, the U.S. Senate overwhelmingly voted in favor of ratifying the treaty,<sup id="cite_ref-359" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-359">&#91;356&#93;</a></sup> providing a major boost to Reagan's popularity in the aftermath of the Iran–Contra affair. A new era of trade and openness between the two powers commenced, and the United States and Soviet Union cooperated on international issues such as the Iran–Iraq War.<sup id="cite_ref-360" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-360">&#91;357&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span id="1989.E2.80.932004:_Post-presidency"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="1989–2004:_Post-presidency">1989–2004: Post-presidency</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1096954695/mw-parser-output/.tmulti"><div class="thumb tmulti tleft"><div class="thumbinner multiimageinner" style="width:392px;max-width:392px"><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:197px;max-width:197px"><div class="thumbimage" style="height:149px;overflow:hidden"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Reagan_and_Gorbachev_in_western_hats_1992.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Reagan and Gorbachev relaxing at Rancho del Cielo in May 1992. Reagan gave Gorbachev a white cowboy hat, which he wore backwards." src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/de/Reagan_and_Gorbachev_in_western_hats_1992.jpg/195px-Reagan_and_Gorbachev_in_western_hats_1992.jpg" decoding="async" width="195" height="150" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/de/Reagan_and_Gorbachev_in_western_hats_1992.jpg/293px-Reagan_and_Gorbachev_in_western_hats_1992.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/de/Reagan_and_Gorbachev_in_western_hats_1992.jpg/390px-Reagan_and_Gorbachev_in_western_hats_1992.jpg 2x" data-file-width="850" data-file-height="652" /></a></span></div><div class="thumbcaption">Reagan and Gorbachev at Rancho del Cielo, 1992</div></div><div class="tsingle" style="width:191px;max-width:191px"><div class="thumbimage" style="height:149px;overflow:hidden"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Reagans_with_USS_Ronald_Reagan_model_1996.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="The Reagans and Newport News Shipbuilding chairman and CEO William Frick standing behind a model of the aircraft carrier USS Ronald Reagan, 1996" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/Reagans_with_USS_Ronald_Reagan_model_1996.jpg/189px-Reagans_with_USS_Ronald_Reagan_model_1996.jpg" decoding="async" width="189" height="150" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/Reagans_with_USS_Ronald_Reagan_model_1996.jpg/284px-Reagans_with_USS_Ronald_Reagan_model_1996.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/Reagans_with_USS_Ronald_Reagan_model_1996.jpg/378px-Reagans_with_USS_Ronald_Reagan_model_1996.jpg 2x" data-file-width="996" data-file-height="792" /></a></span></div><div class="thumbcaption">Nancy and Ronald Reagan with a model of <a href="/wiki/USS_Ronald_Reagan" title="USS Ronald Reagan">USS&#160;<i>Ronald Reagan</i></a>, 1996</div></div></div></div></div>
<p>After leaving the presidency on January 20, 1989,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2000xi_361-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2000xi-361">&#91;358&#93;</a></sup> Ronald and Nancy Reagan lived at <a href="/wiki/668_St._Cloud_Road" title="668 St. Cloud Road">668 St. Cloud Road</a> in <a href="/wiki/Bel_Air,_Los_Angeles" title="Bel Air, Los Angeles">Bel Air</a>, in addition to <a href="/wiki/Rancho_del_Cielo" title="Rancho del Cielo">Rancho del Cielo</a> in <a href="/wiki/Santa_Barbara,_California" title="Santa Barbara, California">Santa Barbara</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard2012180_362-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard2012180-362">&#91;359&#93;</a></sup> He received <a href="/wiki/List_of_accolades_received_by_Ronald_Reagan" class="mw-redirect" title="List of accolades received by Ronald Reagan">multiple awards and honors</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-363" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-363">&#91;360&#93;</a></sup> and received generous payments for speaking engagements. In 1991, the <a href="/wiki/Ronald_Reagan_Presidential_Library" title="Ronald Reagan Presidential Library">Ronald Reagan Presidential Library</a> opened. Reagan also addressed the <a href="/wiki/1992_Republican_National_Convention" title="1992 Republican National Convention">1992 Republican National Convention</a> "to inspire allegiance to the party regulars";<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard2012181–182_364-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard2012181–182-364">&#91;361&#93;</a></sup> publicly favored the <a href="/wiki/Brady_Bill" class="mw-redirect" title="Brady Bill">Brady Bill</a>, drawing criticism from gun control opponents;<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015717–718_365-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015717–718-365">&#91;362&#93;</a></sup> a <a href="/wiki/Constitutional_amendment" title="Constitutional amendment">constitutional amendment</a> requiring a balanced budget; and the repeal of the <a href="/wiki/22nd_Amendment" class="mw-redirect" title="22nd Amendment">22nd Amendment</a>. His final public speech occurred on February 3, 1994, during a tribute to him in Washington, D.C.; his last major public appearance was at the <a href="/wiki/Funeral_of_Richard_Nixon" class="mw-redirect" title="Funeral of Richard Nixon">funeral of Richard Nixon</a> on April 27, 1994.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard2012181–182_364-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard2012181–182-364">&#91;361&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In August 1994, Reagan was diagnosed with <a href="/wiki/Alzheimer%27s_disease" title="Alzheimer&#39;s disease">Alzheimer's disease</a>, which he announced through a handwritten letter in November.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2000xiv_366-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2000xiv-366">&#91;363&#93;</a></sup> There was speculation over how long he had demonstrated symptoms of mental degeneration,<sup id="cite_ref-367" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-367">&#91;364&#93;</a></sup> but lay observations that he suffered from Alzheimer's while still in office have been widely refuted by medical experts;<sup id="cite_ref-368" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-368">&#91;365&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-369" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-369">&#91;366&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-sr_370-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-sr-370">&#91;367&#93;</a></sup> his doctors said that he first began exhibiting overt symptoms of the illness in late 1992<sup id="cite_ref-NYT_2004/06/15_371-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-NYT_2004/06/15-371">&#91;368&#93;</a></sup> or 1993.<sup id="cite_ref-sr_370-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-sr-370">&#91;367&#93;</a></sup> Over time, the disease destroyed Reagan's mental capacity. By 1997, he was reported to recognize few people other than his wife, though he continued to walk through parks and on beaches, play golf, and visit his office in nearby <a href="/wiki/Century_City" title="Century City">Century City</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-sr_370-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-sr-370">&#91;367&#93;</a></sup> Eventually, his family decided that he would live in quiet semi-isolation with his wife.<sup id="cite_ref-372" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-372">&#91;369&#93;</a></sup> By the end of 2003, Reagan had lost his ability to speak and was mostly confined to his bed, no longer able to recognize any family members.<sup id="cite_ref-373" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-373">&#91;370&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Death_and_funeral">Death and funeral</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Death_and_state_funeral_of_Ronald_Reagan" title="Death and state funeral of Ronald Reagan">Death and state funeral of Ronald Reagan</a></div>
<p>Reagan died of <a href="/wiki/Pneumonia" title="Pneumonia">pneumonia</a>, complicated by Alzheimer's,<sup id="cite_ref-Neuman_374-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Neuman-374">&#91;371&#93;</a></sup> at his home in Los Angeles, on June 5, 2004.<sup id="cite_ref-DrehleReaganDies_375-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-DrehleReaganDies-375">&#91;372&#93;</a></sup> President <a href="/wiki/George_W._Bush" title="George W. Bush">George W. Bush</a> called Reagan's death "a sad hour in the life of America".<sup id="cite_ref-Neuman_374-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Neuman-374">&#91;371&#93;</a></sup> His public funeral was held in the <a href="/wiki/Washington_National_Cathedral" title="Washington National Cathedral">Washington National Cathedral</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015731_376-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015731-376">&#91;373&#93;</a></sup> where eulogies were given by Margaret Thatcher, <a href="/wiki/Brian_Mulroney" title="Brian Mulroney">Brian Mulroney</a>, George H. W. Bush, and George W. Bush.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard2012184_377-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard2012184-377">&#91;374&#93;</a></sup> Other world leaders attended including Mikhail Gorbachev and <a href="/wiki/Lech_Wa%C5%82%C4%99sa" title="Lech Wałęsa">Lech Wałęsa</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015732_378-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015732-378">&#91;375&#93;</a></sup> Reagan was interred at his presidential library.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard2012184_377-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard2012184-377">&#91;374&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Legacy">Legacy</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/List_of_things_named_after_Ronald_Reagan" title="List of things named after Ronald Reagan">List of things named after Ronald Reagan</a> and <a href="/wiki/Cultural_depictions_of_Ronald_Reagan" title="Cultural depictions of Ronald Reagan">Cultural depictions of Ronald Reagan</a></div>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Historical_reputation">Historical reputation</span></h3>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:View_of_the_Reagan_Library_from_the_south.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="A view of the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library from the south" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/View_of_the_Reagan_Library_from_the_south.jpg/220px-View_of_the_Reagan_Library_from_the_south.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="146" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/View_of_the_Reagan_Library_from_the_south.jpg/330px-View_of_the_Reagan_Library_from_the_south.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/View_of_the_Reagan_Library_from_the_south.jpg/440px-View_of_the_Reagan_Library_from_the_south.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3300" data-file-height="2186" /></a><figcaption>The Ronald Reagan Presidential Library</figcaption></figure>
<p>In 2008, British historian M. J. Heale summarized that scholars had reached a broad consensus in which "Reagan rehabilitated conservatism, turned the country to the right, practiced a '<a href="/wiki/Pragmatic_conservatism" title="Pragmatic conservatism">pragmatic conservatism</a>' that balanced ideology with the constraints of government, revived faith in the presidency and American self-respect, and contributed to critically ending the Cold War",<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHenry2009933–934_379-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHenry2009933–934-379">&#91;376&#93;</a></sup> which ended with the <a href="/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_Soviet_Union" title="Dissolution of the Soviet Union">dissolution of the Soviet Union</a> in 1991.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2000759Brands2015720_380-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2000759Brands2015720-380">&#91;377&#93;</a></sup> Many conservative and liberal scholars have agreed that Reagan has been the most influential president since Roosevelt, leaving his imprint on American politics, diplomacy, culture, and economics through his effective communication of his conservative agenda and pragmatic compromising.<sup id="cite_ref-381" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-381">&#91;378&#93;</a></sup> During the initial years of Reagan's post-presidency, historical rankings <a href="/wiki/Historical_rankings_of_presidents_of_the_United_States" title="Historical rankings of presidents of the United States">placed his presidency</a> in the twenties.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPatterson2003360Nichols2012282_382-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPatterson2003360Nichols2012282-382">&#91;379&#93;</a></sup> Throughout the 2000s and 2010s, his presidency was often placed in the top ten.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTENichols2012284Johns20151–2_383-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTENichols2012284Johns20151–2-383">&#91;380&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-384" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-384">&#91;381&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Many proponents, including his Cold War contemporaries,<sup id="cite_ref-385" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-385">&#91;382&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKupelian201070Fallon2017182Hampson2018230_386-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKupelian201070Fallon2017182Hampson2018230-386">&#91;383&#93;</a></sup> believe that his defense policies, economic policies, military policies, and hard-line rhetoric against the Soviet Union and communism, together with his summits with Gorbachev, played a significant part in ending the Cold War.<sup id="cite_ref-American_Dreamer_387-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-American_Dreamer-387">&#91;384&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Knopf_287-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Knopf-287">&#91;284&#93;</a></sup> Professor Jeffrey Knopf argues that while Reagan's practice of referring to the Soviet Union as "evil" probably made no difference to the Soviet leaders, it possibly gave encouragement to Eastern European citizens who opposed their communist regimes.<sup id="cite_ref-Knopf_287-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Knopf-287">&#91;284&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Truman_Doctrine" title="Truman Doctrine">President Truman's policy of containment</a> is also regarded as a force behind the fall of the Soviet Union, and the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan undermined the Soviet system itself.<sup id="cite_ref-Reagan&#39;s_role_exaggerated_388-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Reagan&#39;s_role_exaggerated-388">&#91;385&#93;</a></sup> Nevertheless, <a href="/wiki/Melvyn_P._Leffler" title="Melvyn P. Leffler">Melvyn P. Leffler</a> called Reagan "Gorbachev's minor, yet indispensable partner, setting the framework for the dramatic changes that neither anticipated happening anytime soon".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTELeffler202137_389-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeffler202137-389">&#91;386&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Critics, for example Paul Krugman, note Reagan's tenure as having begun a period of increased income inequality, sometimes called the "<a href="/wiki/Great_Divergence_(inequality)" title="Great Divergence (inequality)">Great Divergence</a>". Krugman also views Reagan as having initiated the ideology of the current-day Republican Party, which he feels is led by "radicals" who seek to "undo the twentieth century" gains in income equality and unionization.<sup id="cite_ref-390" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-390">&#91;387&#93;</a></sup> Others, such as Nixon's <a href="/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce" title="United States Secretary of Commerce">Secretary of Commerce</a> <a href="/wiki/Peter_George_Peterson" class="mw-redirect" title="Peter George Peterson">Peter G. Peterson</a>, also criticize what they feel was not just Reagan's fiscal irresponsibility, but also ushering in an era where tax cutting "became the GOP's core platform". With resulting deficits and GOP leaders (speciously in Peterson's opinion) arguing supply-side gains would enable the country to "grow" its way out of deficits.<sup id="cite_ref-391" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-391">&#91;388&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Reagan was known for storytelling and humor,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015734_392-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015734-392">&#91;389&#93;</a></sup> which involved puns<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon200097_393-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon200097-393">&#91;390&#93;</a></sup> and self-deprecation.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998204_394-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998204-394">&#91;391&#93;</a></sup> Reagan also often emphasized <a href="/wiki/Family_values" title="Family values">family values</a>, despite being the first president to have been divorced.<sup id="cite_ref-395" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-395">&#91;392&#93;</a></sup> He showed the ability to comfort Americans during the aftermath of the <a href="/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster" title="Space Shuttle Challenger disaster">Space Shuttle <i>Challenger</i> disaster</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodard2012166_396-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodard2012166-396">&#91;393&#93;</a></sup> Reagan's ability to talk about substantive issues with understandable terms and to focus on mainstream American concerns earned him the laudatory moniker the "Great Communicator".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2000751_397-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2000751-397">&#91;394&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2015734_392-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2015734-392">&#91;389&#93;</a></sup> He also earned the nickname "Teflon President" in that public perceptions of him were not substantially tarnished by the <a href="/wiki/Reagan_administration_scandals" class="mw-redirect" title="Reagan administration scandals">multitude of controversies that arose during his administration</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998112_398-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPemberton1998112-398">&#91;395&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECannon2000182_399-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECannon2000182-399">&#91;396&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Political_influence">Political influence</span></h3>
<p>Reagan led <a href="/wiki/Reagan_coalition" title="Reagan coalition">a new conservative movement</a>, altering the political dynamic of the United States.<sup id="cite_ref-legacy-cnn_400-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-legacy-cnn-400">&#91;397&#93;</a></sup> Conservatism became the dominant ideology for Republicans, displacing the party's faction of liberals and moderates.<sup id="cite_ref-401" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-401">&#91;398&#93;</a></sup> In his time, men began voting more Republican, and women began voting more Democrat – a gender distinction that has persisted.<sup id="cite_ref-legacy-cnn_400-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-legacy-cnn-400">&#91;397&#93;</a></sup> He was supported by young voters, an allegiance that shifted many of them to the party.<sup id="cite_ref-402" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-402">&#91;399&#93;</a></sup> He attempted to appeal to black voters in 1980,<sup id="cite_ref-403" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-403">&#91;400&#93;</a></sup> but would receive the lowest black vote for a Republican presidential candidate at the time.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEShull199340_404-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShull199340-404">&#91;401&#93;</a></sup> Throughout Reagan's presidency, Republicans were unable to gain complete control of Congress.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHeclo2008570_405-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHeclo2008570-405">&#91;402&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The period of American history most dominated by Reagan and his policies (particularly on taxes, welfare, defense, the federal judiciary, and the Cold War) is known as the <a href="/wiki/Reagan_era" title="Reagan era">Reagan era</a>, which suggests that the "Reagan Revolution" had a lasting impact on the United States in domestic and foreign policy. The <a href="/wiki/Bill_Clinton_administration" class="mw-redirect" title="Bill Clinton administration">Bill Clinton administration</a> is often treated as an extension of the era, as is the <a href="/wiki/George_W._Bush_administration" class="mw-redirect" title="George W. Bush administration">George W. Bush administration</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-406" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-406">&#91;403&#93;</a></sup> Since 1988, <a href="/wiki/List_of_United_States_Republican_Party_presidential_tickets" title="List of United States Republican Party presidential tickets">Republican presidential candidates</a> have invoked <a href="/wiki/Political_positions_of_Ronald_Reagan" title="Political positions of Ronald Reagan">Reagan's policies and beliefs</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-agpi_407-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-agpi-407">&#91;404&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Carlos_Lozada_(journalist)" title="Carlos Lozada (journalist)">Carlos Lozada</a> noted Trump's praising of Reagan in a book he published during <a href="/wiki/Donald_Trump_2016_presidential_campaign" title="Donald Trump 2016 presidential campaign">his 2016 campaign</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-408" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-408">&#91;405&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
